# mime_guess2 - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/mime_guess2/

## Expand description

Guessing of MIME types by file extension.

Uses a static list of file-extension : MIME type mappings.

```
// the file doesn't have to exist, it just looks at the path
let guess = mime_guess2::from_path("some_file.gif");
assert_eq!(guess.first(), Some(mime::IMAGE_GIF));
```
[§](https://docs.rs#note-mime-types-returned-are-not-stableguaranteed)Note: MIME Types Returned Are Not Stable/Guaranteed

The media types returned for a given extension are not considered to be part of the crate’s
stable API and are often updated in patch

 (`x.y.[z + 1]`) releases to be as correct as
possible.

Additionally, only the extensions of paths/filenames are inspected in order to guess the MIME type. The file that may or may not reside at that path may or may not be a valid file of the returned MIME type. Be wary of unsafe or un-validated assumptions about file structure or length.

## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub extern crate`- [mime](https://docs.rs/mime/0.3.17/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/mime/index.html);

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Iter](https://docs.rs/struct.Iter.html)
- An iterator over the `Mime`types of a`MimeGuess`.
- [IterRaw](https://docs.rs/struct.IterRaw.html)
- An iterator over the raw media type strings of a `MimeGuess`.
- [Mime](https://docs.rs/struct.Mime.html)
- A parsed mime or media type.
- [Mime](https://docs.rs/struct.MimeGuess.html)- Guess
- A “guess” of the MIME/Media Type(s) of an extension or path as one or more
`Mime`

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [from_](https://docs.rs/fn.from_ext.html)- ext
- Wrapper of `MimeGuess::from_ext()`
- [from_](https://docs.rs/fn.from_path.html)- path
- Wrapper of `MimeGuess::from_path()`
- [get_](https://docs.rs/fn.get_extensions.html)- extensions
- Get the extensions for a given top-level and sub-level of a MIME type
(`{toplevel}/{sublevel}`).
- [get_](https://docs.rs/fn.get_mime_extensions.html)- mime_ - extensions
- Get a list of known extensions for a given `Mime`.
- [get_](https://docs.rs/fn.get_mime_extensions_str.html)- mime_ - extensions_ - str
- Get a list of known extensions for a MIME type string.
- [get_](https://docs.rs/fn.get_mime_type.html)- mime_ - type - Deprecated
- Get the MIME type associated with a file extension.
- [get_](https://docs.rs/fn.get_mime_type_opt.html)- mime_ - type_ - opt - Deprecated
- Get the MIME type associated with a file extension.
- [get_](https://docs.rs/fn.get_mime_type_str.html)- mime_ - type_ - str - Deprecated
- Get the MIME type string associated with a file extension. Case-insensitive.
- [guess_](https://docs.rs/fn.guess_mime_type.html)- mime_ - type - Deprecated
- Guess the MIME type of `path`by its extension (as defined by`Path::extension()`).
- [guess_](https://docs.rs/fn.guess_mime_type_opt.html)- mime_ - type_ - opt - Deprecated
- Guess the MIME type of `path`by its extension (as defined by`Path::extension()`).
- [mime_](https://docs.rs/fn.mime_str_for_path_ext.html)- str_ - for_ - path_ - ext - Deprecated
- Guess the MIME type string of `path`by its extension (as defined by`Path::extension()`).
- [octet_](https://docs.rs/fn.octet_stream.html)- stream - Deprecated
- Get the MIME type for `application/octet-stream`(generic binary stream)

# mime_guess2 2.3.1 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/mime_guess2/latest

MIME/MediaType guessing by file extension. Uses a static map of known file extension -> MIME type mappings.

`mime_guess2`is a fork of`mime_guess`([https://github.com/abonander/mime_guess](https://github.com/abonander/mime_guess)), as`mime_guess`is not actively maintained.

**Returning Contributors: New Requirements for Submissions Below**

##### Required Rust Version: 1.85.1

### Versioning

Due to a mistaken premature release, `mime_guess2` currently publicly depends on a pre-1.0 `mime`,
which means `mime` upgrades are breaking changes and necessitate a major version bump.
Refer to the following table to find a version of `mime_guess2` which matches your version of `mime`:

| `mime`version | `mime_guess2`version |
|---|---|
| `0.1.x, 0.2.x` | `1.x.y` |
| `0.3.x` | `2.x.y` |

#### Note: MIME Types Returned Are Not Stable/Guaranteed

The media types returned for a given extension are not considered to be part of the crate's
stable API and are often updated in patch (`x.y.z + 1`) releases to be as correct as possible. MIME
changes are backported to previous major releases on a best-effort basis.

Note that only the extensions of paths/filenames are inspected in order to guess the MIME type. The file that may or may not reside at that path may or may not be a valid file of the returned MIME type. Be wary of unsafe or un-validated assumptions about file structure or length.

An extension may also have multiple applicable MIME types. When more than one is returned, the first is considered to be the most "correct"--see below for elaboration.

## Contributing

#### Adding or correcting MIME types for extensions

Is the MIME type for a file extension wrong or missing? Great! Well, not great for us, but great for you if you'd like to open a pull request!

The file extension -> MIME type mappings are listed in `src/mime_types.rs`.
**The list is sorted lexicographically by file extension, and all extensions are lowercase (where applicable).**
The former is necessary to support fallback to binary search when the
`phf-map` feature is turned off, and for the maintainers' sanity.
The latter is only for consistency's sake; the search is case-insensitive.

Simply add or update the appropriate string pair(s) to make the correction(s) needed.
Run `cargo test` to make sure the library continues to work correctly.

#### Important! Citing the corrected MIME type

When opening a pull request, please include a link to an official document or RFC noting
the correct MIME type for the file type in question **in the commit message** so
that the commit history can be used as an audit trail.

Though we're only guessing here, we like to be as correct as we can. It makes it much easier to vet your contribution if we don't have to search for corroborating material.

#### Multiple MIME types per extension

As of `2.0.0`, multiple MIME types per extension are supported. The first MIME type in the list for
a given extension should be the most "correct" so users who only care about getting a single MIME
type can use the `first*()` methods.

The definition of "correct" is open to debate, however. In the author's opinion this should be whatever is defined by the latest IETF RFC for the given file format, or otherwise explicitly supercedes all others.

If an official IANA registration replaces an older "experimental" style media type, please place the new type before the old type in the list, but keep the old type for reference:

```
- ("md", &["text/x-markdown"]),
+ ("md", &["text/markdown", "text/x-markdown"]),
```
#### Changes to the API or operation of the crate

We're open to changes to the crate's API or its inner workings, breaking or not, if it improves the overall operation, efficiency, or ergonomics of the crate. However, it would be a good idea to open an issue on the repository so we can discuss your proposed changes and decide how best to approach them.

## License

MIT (See the `LICENSE` file in this repository for more information.)

# mime - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/mime/^0.3/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#mime)Mime

Mime is now Media Type, technically, but `Mime` is more immediately
understandable, so the main type here is `Mime`.

[§](https://docs.rs#what-is-mime)What is Mime?

Example mime string: `text/plain`

```
let plain_text: mime::Mime = "text/plain".parse().unwrap();
assert_eq!(plain_text, mime::TEXT_PLAIN);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#inspecting-mimes)Inspecting Mimes

```
let mime = mime::TEXT_PLAIN;
match (mime.type_(), mime.subtype()) {
    (mime::TEXT, mime::PLAIN) => println!("plain text!"),
    (mime::TEXT, _) => println!("structured text"),
    _ => println!("not text"),
}
```

# phf - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/phf/^0.11/

## Expand description

Rust-PHF is a library to generate efficient lookup tables at compile time using
[perfect hash functions](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perfect_hash_function).

It currently uses the
[CHD algorithm](http://cmph.sourceforge.net/papers/esa09.pdf) and can generate
a 100,000 entry map in roughly .4 seconds.

MSRV (minimum supported rust version) is Rust 1.61.

[§](https://docs.rs#usage)Usage

PHF data structures can be constructed via either the procedural
macros in the `phf_macros` crate or code generation supported by the
`phf_codegen` crate. If you prefer macros, you can easily use them by
enabling the `macros` feature of the `phf` crate, like:

```
 [dependencies]
 phf = { version = "0.11", features = ["macros"] }
```
To compile the `phf` crate with a dependency on
libcore instead of libstd, enabling use in environments where libstd
will not work, set `default-features = false` for the dependency:

```
[dependencies]
# to use `phf` in `no_std` environments
phf = { version = "0.11", default-features = false }
```
[§](https://docs.rs#example-with-the-macros-feature-enabled)Example (with the `macros` feature enabled)

```
use phf::phf_map;
#[derive(Clone)]
pub enum Keyword {
    Loop,
    Continue,
    Break,
    Fn,
    Extern,
}
static KEYWORDS: phf::Map<&'static str, Keyword> = phf_map! {
    "loop" => Keyword::Loop,
    "continue" => Keyword::Continue,
    "break" => Keyword::Break,
    "fn" => Keyword::Fn,
    "extern" => Keyword::Extern,
};
pub fn parse_keyword(keyword: &str) -> Option<Keyword> {
    KEYWORDS.get(keyword).cloned()
}
```
Alternatively, you can use the [ phf_codegen](https://docs.rs/phf_codegen) crate to generate PHF datatypes
in a build script.

[§](https://docs.rs#note)Note

Currently, the macro syntax has some limitations and may not
work as you want. See [#183](https://github.com/rust-phf/rust-phf/issues/183) or [#196](https://github.com/rust-phf/rust-phf/issues/196) for example.

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [map](https://docs.rs/map/index.html)
- An immutable map constructed at compile time.
- [ordered_](https://docs.rs/ordered_map/index.html)- map
- An order-preserving immutable map constructed at compile time.
- [ordered_](https://docs.rs/ordered_set/index.html)- set
- An order-preserving immutable set constructed at compile time.
- [set](https://docs.rs/set/index.html)
- An immutable set constructed at compile time.

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [phf_map](https://docs.rs/macro.phf_map.html)
- Macro to create a `static`(compile-time)`Map`
- [phf_](https://docs.rs/macro.phf_ordered_map.html)- ordered_ - map
- Macro to create a `static`(compile-time)`OrderedMap`
- [phf_](https://docs.rs/macro.phf_ordered_set.html)- ordered_ - set
- Macro to create a `static`(compile-time)`OrderedSet`
- [phf_set](https://docs.rs/macro.phf_set.html)
- Macro to create a `static`(compile-time)`Set`

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Map](https://docs.rs/struct.Map.html)
- An immutable map constructed at compile time.
- [Ordered](https://docs.rs/struct.OrderedMap.html)- Map
- An order-preserving immutable map constructed at compile time.
- [Ordered](https://docs.rs/struct.OrderedSet.html)- Set
- An order-preserving immutable set constructed at compile time.
- [Set](https://docs.rs/struct.Set.html)
- An immutable set constructed at compile time.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [PhfHash](https://docs.rs/trait.PhfHash.html)
- A trait implemented by types which can be used in PHF data structures.

# unicase - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/unicase/^2.8.1/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#unicase)UniCase

UniCase provides a way of specifying strings that are case-insensitive.

UniCase supports full [Unicode case
folding](https://www.w3.org/International/wiki/Case_folding). It can also
utilize faster ASCII case comparisons, if both strings are ASCII.

Using the `UniCase::new()` constructor will check the string to see if it
is all ASCII. When a `UniCase` is compared against another, if both are
ASCII, it will use the faster comparison.

There also exists the `Ascii` type in this crate, which will always assume
to use the ASCII case comparisons, if the encoding is already known.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use unicase::UniCase;
let a = UniCase::new("Maße");
let b = UniCase::new("MASSE");
let c = UniCase::new("mase");
assert_eq!(a, b);
assert!(b != c);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#ascii)Ascii

```
use unicase::Ascii;
let a = Ascii::new("foobar");
let b = Ascii::new("FoObAr");
assert_eq!(a, b);
```

# divan - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/divan/^0.1.17/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#sponsor)Sponsor

If you or your company find Divan valuable, consider [sponsoring on
GitHub](https://github.com/sponsors/nvzqz) or [donating via
PayPal](https://paypal.me/nvzqz). Sponsorships help me progress on what’s
possible with benchmarking in Rust.

[§](https://docs.rs#guide)Guide

A guide is being worked on. In the meantime, see:

[§](https://docs.rs#getting-started)Getting Started

Divan `0.1.21` requires Rust `1.80.0` or later.

-
Add the following to your project’s `Cargo.toml``[dev-dependencies] divan = "0.1.21" [[bench]] name = "example" harness = false`
-
Create a benchmarks file at `benches/example.rs`[1](https://docs.rs#fn1)`fn main() { // Run registered benchmarks. divan::main(); } // Register a `fibonacci` function and benchmark it over multiple cases. #[divan::bench(args = [1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32])] fn fibonacci(n: u64) -> u64 { if n <= 1 { 1 } else { fibonacci(n - 2) + fibonacci(n - 1) } }`
-
Run your benchmarks with `cargo bench``example fastest │ slowest │ median │ mean │ samples │ iters ╰─ fibonacci │ │ │ │ │ ├─ 1 0.626 ns │ 1.735 ns │ 0.657 ns │ 0.672 ns │ 100 │ 819200 ├─ 2 2.767 ns │ 3.154 ns │ 2.788 ns │ 2.851 ns │ 100 │ 204800 ├─ 4 6.816 ns │ 7.671 ns │ 7.061 ns │ 7.167 ns │ 100 │ 102400 ├─ 8 57.31 ns │ 62.51 ns │ 57.96 ns │ 58.55 ns │ 100 │ 12800 ├─ 16 2.874 µs │ 3.812 µs │ 2.916 µs │ 3.006 µs │ 100 │ 200 ╰─ 32 6.267 ms │ 6.954 ms │ 6.283 ms │ 6.344 ms │ 100 │ 100`

See [ #[divan::bench]](https://docs.rs/attr.bench.html) for info on benchmark function registration.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

Practical example benchmarks can be found in the [ examples/benches](https://github.com/nvzqz/divan/tree/main/examples/benches)
directory. These can be benchmarked locally by running:

```
git clone https://github.com/nvzqz/divan.git
cd divan
cargo bench -q -p examples --all-features
```
More thorough usage examples can be found in the [ #[divan::bench] documentation](https://docs.rs/attr.bench.html#examples).

Like the Rust project, this library may be used under either the
[MIT License](https://github.com/nvzqz/divan/blob/main/LICENSE-MIT) or
[Apache License (Version 2.0)](https://github.com/nvzqz/divan/blob/main/LICENSE-APACHE).

# phf_codegen - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/phf_codegen/^0.11/

## Expand description

A set of builders to generate Rust source for PHF data structures at compile time.

The provided builders are intended to be used in a Cargo build script to generate a Rust source file that will be included in a library at build time.

For more information about `rust-phf` crates, see [the  phf crate’s documentation](https://docs.rs/phf).

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

To use `phf_codegen` on build.rs, you have to add dependencies under `[build-dependencies]`:

```
[build-dependencies]
phf = { version = "0.11.1", default-features = false }
phf_codegen = "0.11.1"
```
Then put code on build.rs:

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
use std::env;
use std::fs::File;
use std::io::{BufWriter, Write};
use std::path::Path;
fn main() {
    let path = Path::new(&env::var("OUT_DIR").unwrap()).join("codegen.rs");
    let mut file = BufWriter::new(File::create(&path).unwrap());
    write!(
        &mut file,
        "static KEYWORDS: phf::Map<&'static str, Keyword> = {}",
        phf_codegen::Map::new()
            .entry("loop", "Keyword::Loop")
            .entry("continue", "Keyword::Continue")
            .entry("break", "Keyword::Break")
            .entry("fn", "Keyword::Fn")
            .entry("extern", "Keyword::Extern")
            .build()
    )
    .unwrap();
    write!(&mut file, ";\n").unwrap();
}
```
and lib.rs:

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
#[derive(Clone)]
enum Keyword {
    Loop,
    Continue,
    Break,
    Fn,
    Extern,
}
include!(concat!(env!("OUT_DIR"), "/codegen.rs"));
pub fn parse_keyword(keyword: &str) -> Option<Keyword> {
    KEYWORDS.get(keyword).cloned()
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#byte-string-keys)Byte-String Keys

Byte strings by default produce references to fixed-size arrays; the compiler needs a hint to coerce them to slices:

build.rs:

```
use std::env;
use std::fs::File;
use std::io::{BufWriter, Write};
use std::path::Path;
fn main() {
    let path = Path::new(&env::var("OUT_DIR").unwrap()).join("codegen.rs");
    let mut file = BufWriter::new(File::create(&path).unwrap());
    writeln!(
        &mut file,
         "static KEYWORDS: phf::Map<&'static [u8], Keyword> = \n{};\n",
         phf_codegen::Map::<&[u8]>::new()
             .entry(b"loop", "Keyword::Loop")
             .entry(b"continue", "Keyword::Continue")
             .entry(b"break", "Keyword::Break")
             .entry(b"fn", "Keyword::Fn")
             .entry(b"extern", "Keyword::Extern")
             .build()
    ).unwrap();
}
```
lib.rs:

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
#[derive(Clone)]
enum Keyword {
    Loop,
    Continue,
    Break,
    Fn,
    Extern,
}
include!(concat!(env!("OUT_DIR"), "/codegen.rs"));
pub fn parse_keyword(keyword: &[u8]) -> Option<Keyword> {
    KEYWORDS.get(keyword).cloned()
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#note)Note

The compiler’s stack will overflow when processing extremely long method chains (500+ calls). When generating large PHF data structures, consider looping over the entries or making each call a separate statement:

```
let entries = [("hello", "1"), ("world", "2")];
let mut builder = phf_codegen::Map::new();
for &(key, value) in &entries {
    builder.entry(key, value);
}
// ...
```
```
let mut builder = phf_codegen::Map::new();
builder.entry("hello", "1");
builder.entry("world", "2");
// ...
```

# mime_guess2 - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/mime_guess2/latest/target-redirect/mime_guess2/

## Expand description

Guessing of MIME types by file extension.

Uses a static list of file-extension : MIME type mappings.

```
// the file doesn't have to exist, it just looks at the path
let guess = mime_guess2::from_path("some_file.gif");
assert_eq!(guess.first(), Some(mime::IMAGE_GIF));
```
[§](https://docs.rs#note-mime-types-returned-are-not-stableguaranteed)Note: MIME Types Returned Are Not Stable/Guaranteed

The media types returned for a given extension are not considered to be part of the crate’s
stable API and are often updated in patch

 (`x.y.[z + 1]`) releases to be as correct as
possible.

Additionally, only the extensions of paths/filenames are inspected in order to guess the MIME type. The file that may or may not reside at that path may or may not be a valid file of the returned MIME type. Be wary of unsafe or un-validated assumptions about file structure or length.

## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub extern crate`- [mime](https://docs.rs/mime/0.3.17/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/mime/index.html);

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Iter](https://docs.rs/struct.Iter.html)
- An iterator over the `Mime`types of a`MimeGuess`.
- [IterRaw](https://docs.rs/struct.IterRaw.html)
- An iterator over the raw media type strings of a `MimeGuess`.
- [Mime](https://docs.rs/struct.Mime.html)
- A parsed mime or media type.
- [Mime](https://docs.rs/struct.MimeGuess.html)- Guess
- A “guess” of the MIME/Media Type(s) of an extension or path as one or more
`Mime`

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [from_](https://docs.rs/fn.from_ext.html)- ext
- Wrapper of `MimeGuess::from_ext()`
- [from_](https://docs.rs/fn.from_path.html)- path
- Wrapper of `MimeGuess::from_path()`
- [get_](https://docs.rs/fn.get_extensions.html)- extensions
- Get the extensions for a given top-level and sub-level of a MIME type
(`{toplevel}/{sublevel}`).
- [get_](https://docs.rs/fn.get_mime_extensions.html)- mime_ - extensions
- Get a list of known extensions for a given `Mime`.
- [get_](https://docs.rs/fn.get_mime_extensions_str.html)- mime_ - extensions_ - str
- Get a list of known extensions for a MIME type string.
- [get_](https://docs.rs/fn.get_mime_type.html)- mime_ - type - Deprecated
- Get the MIME type associated with a file extension.
- [get_](https://docs.rs/fn.get_mime_type_opt.html)- mime_ - type_ - opt - Deprecated
- Get the MIME type associated with a file extension.
- [get_](https://docs.rs/fn.get_mime_type_str.html)- mime_ - type_ - str - Deprecated
- Get the MIME type string associated with a file extension. Case-insensitive.
- [guess_](https://docs.rs/fn.guess_mime_type.html)- mime_ - type - Deprecated
- Guess the MIME type of `path`by its extension (as defined by`Path::extension()`).
- [guess_](https://docs.rs/fn.guess_mime_type_opt.html)- mime_ - type_ - opt - Deprecated
- Guess the MIME type of `path`by its extension (as defined by`Path::extension()`).
- [mime_](https://docs.rs/fn.mime_str_for_path_ext.html)- str_ - for_ - path_ - ext - Deprecated
- Guess the MIME type string of `path`by its extension (as defined by`Path::extension()`).
- [octet_](https://docs.rs/fn.octet_stream.html)- stream - Deprecated
- Get the MIME type for `application/octet-stream`(generic binary stream)

# About Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/about

Docs.rs is an
            [open source](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs)
            documentation host for crates of the
            [Rust Programming Language](https://www.rust-lang.org/).
            All libraries published to [crates.io](https://crates.io)
            are documented. If you just published a crate, your crate is likely
            still in [the queue](https://docs.rs/releases/queue).

            The source code of Docs.rs is available on
            [GitHub](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs). If
            you ever encounter an issue, don't hesitate to report it! (And
            thanks in advance!)

Currently running Docs.rs version is: **0.0.0 (964c90a45859fd8f9076e3cbe58470a5a4f4d4f7 2026-07-01 )**

Summaries of the documentation build processes [are available at /releases/](https://docs.rs/releases).

            JavaScript in support of documentation is allowed but not guaranteed to work on docs.rs. What that
            means: If you write documentation that inlines some JavaScript (like
            [KaTeX](https://katex.org/)), that's allowed, and
            will probably work today but may break in the future.

However, it's not allowed to put JavaScript or other content in docs published on docs.rs for the purpose of tracking visitors. For instance, adding Google Analytics scripts, tracking pixels, or site verification for services like Google Search Console. Crates that do this will have the relevant versions removed and may be blocked from docs.rs.

            Docs.rs is run and maintained by the [Docs.rs team](https://www.rust-lang.org/governance/teams/dev-tools#team-docs-rs).
            You can find us in #t-docs-rs on [Zulip](https://rust-lang.zulipchat.com/#narrow/stream/356853-t-docs-rs).

# Builds

Source: https://docs.rs/about/builds

Docs.rs automatically builds documentation for crates released on [crates.io](https://crates.io/).
                It may take a while to build your crate, depending on how many crates are in [the queue](https://docs.rs/releases/queue).

                All crates are built in a sandbox using the nightly release of the Rust compiler.
                The current version in use is `rustc 1.98.0-nightly (c397dae80 2026-07-02)`.

                The README displayed on docs.rs follows Cargo’s `package.readme` rules.
                If `readme` is not set, docs.rs will look for `README.md`, `README.txt`, or `README` in the crate root.
                Set `readme = "path/to/file"` to use a custom file, `readme = true` to use `README.md`, or `readme = false` to disable the README.

                To recognize Docs.rs from your Rust code, you can test for the `docsrs` cfg, e.g.:

```
```
                To recognize Docs.rs from `build.rs` files, you can test for the environment variable `DOCS_RS`, e.g.:

`if var.is_ok `
              All targets other than `x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu` are cross-compiled. For implementation reasons, this is unlikely to change for the foreseeable future.

                You can configure how your crate is built by adding [package metadata](https://docs.rs/metadata) to your `Cargo.toml`, e.g.:

```
[]
 = ["--cfg", "my_cfg"]
```
`#[cfg(my_cfg)]` (not to be confused with `#[cfg(doc)]`) can be used for conditional compilation.
                This approach is also useful for setting
                When you start using docs.rs metadata or `#[cfg(docsrs)]` in your code, you might run into issues
                where your code builds fine locally but fails on docs.rs.
                To avoid this, you can add [ cargo docs-rs](https://github.com/dtolnay/cargo-docs-rs) to
                your test-suite.
                While it doesn't perfectly replicate our build environment, it can catch many common issues.

                The Docs.rs [README](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/blob/master/README.md#build-subcommand) describes how to build
                unpublished crate documentation locally using the same build environment as the Docs.rs build agent.

                Missing dependencies are a common reason for failed builds.
                Docs.rs dependencies are managed through
                [crates-build-env](https://github.com/rust-lang/crates-build-env).
                See [Forge](https://forge.rust-lang.org/docs-rs/add-dependencies.html) for how to add a dependency.

                Most of the sandbox is a read-only file system, including the source directory of your crate and its dependencies.
                If your `build.rs` generates files that are relevant for documentation, consider writing to the
                [cargo output directory](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/environment-variables.html#environment-variables-cargo-sets-for-crates),
                passed in the environment variable `OUT_DIR`.

All the builds are executed inside a sandbox with limited resources. The current limits are:

| Available RAM | 6.44 GB |
| Maximum rustdoc execution time | 15m |
| Maximum size of a build log | 102.4 kB |
| Network access | blocked |
| Maximum number of build targets | 10 |

                If your build fails because it hit one of these limits, please
                [open an issue](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/issues/new/choose)
                to get them increased for your crate.
                Since our build agent has finite resources, we have to consider each case individually. However, there are a few general policies:

If your crate fails to build for a reason not listed here, you can rebuild it from [crates.io](https://crates.io) website as you can see below:

Or you can [file an issue](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/issues) if you think it's a **docs.rs** issue.

# Metadata

Source: https://docs.rs/about/metadata

You can customize docs.rs builds by defining `[package.metadata.docs.rs]`
		table in your crates' `Cargo.toml`.

The available configuration flags you can customize are:

```
[]
 = "test"
[]
# Features to pass to Cargo (default: [])
 = ["feature1", "feature2"]
# Whether to pass `--all-features` to Cargo (default: false)
 = true
# Whether to pass `--no-default-features` to Cargo (default: false)
 = true
# Target to test build on, used as the default landing page (default: "x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu")
#
# Any target supported by rustup can be used.
 = "x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu"
# Targets to build (default: see below)
#
# Any target supported by rustup can be used.
#
# Default targets:
# - x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu
# - aarch64-apple-darwin
# - x86_64-pc-windows-msvc
# - aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu
# - i686-pc-windows-msvc
#
# Set this to `[]` to only build the default target.
#
# If `default-target` is unset, the first element of `targets` is treated as the default target.
# Otherwise, these `targets` are built in addition to the default target.
# If both `default-target` and `targets` are unset,
#   all tier-one targets will be built and `x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu` will be used as the default target.
 = ["aarch64-apple-darwin", "x86_64-pc-windows-msvc"]
# If you want to instead add another target without overwriting the default ones:
 = ["i686-apple-darwin"]
# Additional `RUSTFLAGS` to set (default: [])
 = ["--example-rustc-arg"]
# Additional `RUSTDOCFLAGS` to set (default: [])
 = ["--example-rustdoc-arg"]
# List of command line arguments for `cargo`.
#
# These cannot be a subcommand, they may only be options.
 = ["-Z", "build-std"]
```

# Shorthand URLs

Source: https://docs.rs/about/redirections

Docs.rs uses semver to parse URLs. You can use this feature to access
            crates' documentation easily. Example of URL redirections for
            `clap` crate:

| URL | Redirects to documentation of |
|---|---|
| [docs.rs/clap](https://docs.rs/clap) | Latest version of clap |
| [docs.rs/clap::Command](https://docs.rs/clap::Command) | Latest version of clap, and search for "Command" within the crate |
| [docs.rs/clap/~2](https://docs.rs/clap/%7E2) | 2.* version |
| [docs.rs/clap/~2.9](https://docs.rs/clap/%7E2.9) | 2.9.* version |
| [docs.rs/clap/2.9.3](https://docs.rs/clap/2.9.3) | 2.9.3 version (you don't need `=`unlike semver) |
| [docs.rs/clap/*](https://docs.rs/clap/*) | Latest version of this page (if it still exists). "latest" or "newest" work as well as `*`. |

---

# Download

Source: https://docs.rs/about/download

docs.rs stores the `rustdoc` output in a ZIP file.

                These archives can be used as a base for further processing of
                the documentation for offline readers like Dash or Zeal.
                **They are not directly usable for offline documentation.**

The download is possible for specific or semantic versions:

But also viaTo unpack the ZIP file you need any zip utility that supports PKZIP version 4.6 and BZIP2 & Deflate compression.

The archives will contain all the documentation HTML files for all targets and CSS/JS assets that are specific to the build. The default target will be found at the root, and other targets each in its own subfolder.

                Docs.rs is running rustdoc with `--static-root-path "/-/rustdoc.static/"`,
                which leads to all references to static assets breaking if they are not
                available under that path. Older builds used `--static-root-path "/"`, which
                means you will have to handle both.

                Since we're also adding `--emit=invocation-specific` to our build
                the archives will *not* contain any static assets that are specific to the
                toolchain. For now these will have to be downloaded file-by-file directly
                from docs.rs.

---

# Rustdoc JSON

Source: https://docs.rs/about/rustdoc-json

docs.rs builds & hosts the [ rustdoc JSON](https://doc.rust-lang.org/rustdoc/unstable-features.html#json-output) output.

This structured version of the documentation can be used for inspecting the docs and types of the crate in a programmatic way.

                The JSON file you're downloading might have been built with an older version of `rustdoc`
                so you might have to check the `format_version` attribute to determine how to parse the structure.
                The [ rustdoc-types](https://docs.rs/rustdoc-types/) crate helps with this.

**
                We started building rustdoc JSON on 2025-05-23. So any release before that won't have a download
                available until our rebuilds reached that release.
            **

                The download URLs can be generic or specific, depending on what you need. In case of rebuilds we
                also keep old format versions around. **Until we rebuilt all releases, we might return
                a `404 NOT FOUND` for some.**

By default we use `zstd` compression, which is more space efficient and faster to decompress. For more limited environments we also started supporting `gzip` compression. You can receive gzip by adding `.gz` to the given URL.

Here some URL examples you can use.

| URL | Redirects to JSON download of |
|---|---|
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json) | latest version, default target, latest format-version |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json.gz](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json.gz) | latest version, default target, latest format-version, gzip compression |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json/42](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json/42) | latest version, default target, format-version 42 |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/~4/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/%7E4/json) | latest v4 via semver, default target, latest format-version |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/~4/json.zst](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/%7E4/json.zst) | latest v4 via semver, default target, latest format-version, zstd compression |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/i686-pc-windows-msvc/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/i686-pc-windows-msvc/json) | latest version, windows target, latest format-version |

# mime - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/mime/0.3.17/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/mime/index.html

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#mime)Mime

Mime is now Media Type, technically, but `Mime` is more immediately
understandable, so the main type here is `Mime`.

[§](https://docs.rs#what-is-mime)What is Mime?

Example mime string: `text/plain`

```
let plain_text: mime::Mime = "text/plain".parse().unwrap();
assert_eq!(plain_text, mime::TEXT_PLAIN);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#inspecting-mimes)Inspecting Mimes

```
let mime = mime::TEXT_PLAIN;
match (mime.type_(), mime.subtype()) {
    (mime::TEXT, mime::PLAIN) => println!("plain text!"),
    (mime::TEXT, _) => println!("structured text"),
    _ => println!("not text"),
}
```
## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [From](https://docs.rs/struct.FromStrError.html)- StrError
- An error when parsing a `Mime`from a string.
- [Mime](https://docs.rs/struct.Mime.html)
- A parsed mime or media type.
- [Mime](https://docs.rs/struct.MimeIter.html)- Iter
- An iterator of parsed mime
- [Name](https://docs.rs/struct.Name.html)
- A section of a `Mime`.
- [Params](https://docs.rs/struct.Params.html)
- An iterator over the parameters of a MIME.

# hrdr_editor - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/hrdr-editor/0.2.1/hrdr_editor/

## Expand description

`hrdr-editor` — the FSM-agnostic editing seam.

The rest of hrdr talks only to the [ EditorEngine](https://docs.rs/trait.EditorEngine.html) trait — never to vim
types. The concrete

[wraps the hjkl engine and drives it through](https://docs.rs/struct.VimEngine.html)

`VimEngine``hjkl_vim::dispatch_input`. When hjkl’s pluggable-FSM work (epic
#265) lands a vscode/helix discipline, add a sibling `EditorEngine` impl
and the TUI swaps it in with zero churn — it reads `mode_label()` /
`is_insert()` (projected from hjkl’s FSM-agnostic `CoarseMode`), not
`VimMode`.## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Editor](https://docs.rs/struct.EditorKey.html)- Key
- The seam’s renderer-agnostic key DTO — hjkl’s own toolkit-neutral
`Input { key, ctrl, alt, shift }`, re-exported so consumers never touch hjkl types directly. A key press with modifier flags. The vim engine reads modifiers directly off this struct (e.g.`input.ctrl && input.key == Key::Char('d')`).
- [Hrdr](https://docs.rs/struct.HrdrHost.html)- Host
- [Plain](https://docs.rs/struct.PlainEngine.html)- Engine
- A plain UTF-8 text buffer with a char-index cursor.
- [VimEngine](https://docs.rs/struct.VimEngine.html)
- The default discipline: hjkl’s vim FSM.

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Editor](https://docs.rs/enum.EditorKeyCode.html)- KeyCode
- The seam’s renderer-agnostic key DTO — hjkl’s own toolkit-neutral
`Input { key, ctrl, alt, shift }`, re-exported so consumers never touch hjkl types directly. A key code, mirroring the subset of [`crossterm::event::KeyCode`] the vim engine actually consumes.`Null`is the conventional sentinel for “no input” (matching the previous`tui_textarea::Key`shape) so call sites can early-return on unsupported keys.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Editor](https://docs.rs/trait.EditorEngine.html)- Engine
- A pluggable editing discipline — the renderer-agnostic core of the seam.
- [TuiEditor](https://docs.rs/trait.TuiEditorEngine.html)- Engine
- What the TUI hosts: both halves of the seam.
- [TuiRender](https://docs.rs/trait.TuiRender.html)
- The terminal renderer half of the seam (ratatui). Kept out of
`EditorEngine`

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [key_](https://docs.rs/fn.key_from_crossterm.html)- from_ - crossterm
- Convert a crossterm key event to the seam’s `EditorKey``None`for key-release events, which must not reach the engines (terminals reporting them would double keystrokes).

# hrdr_agent - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/hrdr-agent/0.2.1/hrdr_agent/

## Expand description

`hrdr-agent` — the agentic loop.

Drives an OpenAI-compatible model through tool calls until a coding task is
complete: stream a turn, execute any requested tools, feed the results back,
repeat. Emits [ AgentEvent](https://docs.rs/enum.AgentEvent.html)s for a UI (or stdout) to render live.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Agent](https://docs.rs/struct.Agent.html)
- A running agent: model client + tools + conversation state.
- [Agent](https://docs.rs/struct.AgentConfig.html)- Config
- Agent configuration.
- [Checkpoint](https://docs.rs/struct.CheckpointInfo.html)- Info
- One revertible checkpoint (a turn that changed files).
- [File](https://docs.rs/struct.FileCheckpoints.html)- Checkpoints
- A disk-backed store of per-turn file pre-images.
- [Guardrail](https://docs.rs/struct.GuardrailConfig.html)- Config
- One user-defined shell guardrail from a `[[guardrails]]`config entry: commands matching`pattern`(a regex) are rejected with`message`. Applied on top of the built-in rules (`hrdr_tools::default_guardrails`).
- [Hook](https://docs.rs/struct.HookConfig.html)- Config
- One post-edit hook from a `[[hooks]]`config entry: after tool`on`(`edit`,`write_file`, or`*`) successfully mutates a file matching`glob`, run shell command`run`(`{path}`is substituted). Formatters, mostly. Failures surface as warnings in the tool result, never as errors.
- [Message](https://docs.rs/struct.Message.html)
- A single chat message. Used for both request and response — `content`is optional because assistant turns that only call tools carry no text.
- [Provider](https://docs.rs/struct.ProviderConfig.html)- Config
- A user-defined provider from `[providers.<name>]`in config.
- [Resolved](https://docs.rs/struct.ResolvedProvider.html)- Provider
- A fully-resolved provider preset.
- [Session](https://docs.rs/struct.Session.html)
- A saved conversation.
- [Session](https://docs.rs/struct.SessionMeta.html)- Meta
- Lightweight directory listing entry.
- [Todo](https://docs.rs/struct.Todo.html)
- A single TODO item tracked by `todo_write`.

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Agent](https://docs.rs/enum.AgentEvent.html)- Event
- Events emitted as a turn progresses.
- [Config](https://docs.rs/enum.ConfigValue.html)- Value
- A value to persist into the user config file.
- [Message](https://docs.rs/enum.MessageRole.html)- Role
- Message author role.

## Constants[§](https://docs.rs#constants)

- [DEFAULT_](https://docs.rs/constant.DEFAULT_AUTO_COMPACT.html)- AUTO_ - COMPACT
- Default auto-compaction trigger: 85% of the context window (leaves headroom so the next turn doesn’t overflow).

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [builtin_](https://docs.rs/fn.builtin_provider.html)- provider
- Resolve a built-in provider name (case-insensitive).
- [config_](https://docs.rs/fn.config_dir.html)- dir
- `hrdr`’s config directory —- `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/hrdr`, default- `~/.config/hrdr`(cross-platform via home-dir detection). Shared by- `config.toml`loading and the global- `AGENTS.md`lookup so the two can’t diverge.
- [config_](https://docs.rs/fn.config_file_path.html)- file_ - path
- Path to the user config file (`~/.config/hrdr/config.toml`), if`HOME`is set.
- [cwd_](https://docs.rs/fn.cwd_slug.html)- slug
- Slug for a working directory — the per-cwd subdirectory name. The full path
is flattened (e.g. `/home/me/Projects/foo`→`home-me-projects-foo`).
- [gather_](https://docs.rs/fn.gather_agent_docs.html)- agent_ - docs
- Collect project instructions from `AGENTS.md`files, walking from`cwd`up to the filesystem root, plus an optional global`~/.config/hrdr/AGENTS.md`. Less specific files (global, then ancestors) come first so nearer files override by appearing later. Returns`None`if nothing is found.
- [in_](https://docs.rs/fn.in_git_repo.html)- git_ - repo
- Whether `cwd`(or an ancestor) is inside a git repo.`.git`may be a directory (normal) or a file (worktrees/submodules).
- [list_](https://docs.rs/fn.list_sessions.html)- sessions
- List saved sessions across every working directory, newest first. Also
picks up legacy flat-layout files written directly under `sessions/`.
- [parse_](https://docs.rs/fn.parse_env_bool.html)- env_ - bool
- Parse a boolean-ish env value; `None`(leave the current value) if it’s not one of the recognized on/off spellings. Parse a boolean setting from a config/CLI/env string, accepting the common spellings (`1`/`0`,`true`/`false`,`on`/`off`,`yes`/`no`, case-insensitive). Returns`None`for anything unrecognized so callers can leave the current value unchanged.
- [persist_](https://docs.rs/fn.persist_setting.html)- setting
- Set `key = value`in the user config file (creating it if needed), preserving existing keys, ordering, and comments. Returns the file path.
- [remove_](https://docs.rs/fn.remove_setting.html)- setting
- Remove `key`from the user config file (if present). Returns the file path.
- [render_](https://docs.rs/fn.render_system.html)- system
- Render the agent system prompt for the given tool set and working directory.
`instructions`is the gathered AGENTS.md content (see`gather_agent_docs`
- [resolve_](https://docs.rs/fn.resolve_session.html)- session
- Resolve a `/resume`argument to`(id, Session)`. Looks in`cwd`’s directory first (by file id), then scans every directory — preferring the current`cwd`— matching the file id or the display`name`(case-insensitive, e.g. after`/rename`).
- [session_](https://docs.rs/fn.session_dir.html)- dir
- The per-cwd directory a session lives in.
- [sessions_](https://docs.rs/fn.sessions_dir.html)- dir
- `$XDG_DATA_HOME/hrdr/sessions`, or- `~/.local/share/hrdr/sessions`.
- [unique_](https://docs.rs/fn.unique_session_id.html)- session_ - id
- A collision-free file id (within `cwd`’s directory) derived from`name`: the slug, then`slug-2`,`slug-3`, … if files already exist.

# sandogasa_meetbot - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/sandogasa-meetbot/0.15.3/sandogasa_meetbot/

## Expand description

HTTP client for [meetbot.fedoraproject.org](https://meetbot.fedoraproject.org/)’s
meeting search endpoint.

Meetbot exposes a single lightweight JSON endpoint for the “Search for conversations” UI in its web frontend. This crate wraps that endpoint behind a typed client.

```
use sandogasa_meetbot::Meetbot;
let client = Meetbot::new();
for meeting in client.search("centos-hyperscale-sig")? {
    println!("{} {}", meeting.datetime, meeting.summary_url);
}
```
## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

## Constants[§](https://docs.rs#constants)

- [DEFAULT_](https://docs.rs/constant.DEFAULT_BASE_URL.html)- BASE_ - URL
- Default production base URL for meetbot’s web frontend.
- [PUBLIC_](https://docs.rs/constant.PUBLIC_ARTEFACT_BASE.html)- ARTEFACT_ - BASE
- Default base URL used for public meeting artefacts (log /
summary HTML). Distinct from the web frontend: the JSON
endpoint returns URLs on `meetbot-raw.fedoraproject.org`, but users typically want to link to the public-facing`meetbot.fedoraproject.org`host instead.`Meetbot::search`applies this rewrite.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [dedup_](https://docs.rs/fn.dedup_by_longest_log.html)- by_ - longest_ - log
- Collapse same-day duplicates in a meeting list by keeping
the entry whose `logs_url`is the largest, as a rough proxy for “the meeting that actually happened” when`!startmeeting`was run multiple times (on the same channel, or across overlapping channels) on a single day.`on_warning`is invoked once per collapsed group with`(winner, dropped)`so the caller can surface it to the user.

# camel_component_api - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/camel-component-api/0.22.0/camel_component_api/

## Expand description

camel-component-api — traits and types for building Camel components.

Provides the core abstractions (`Component`, `Endpoint`, `Consumer`, `Producer`)
that every rust-camel component implements. Also re-exports commonly-used types
from `camel-api` and `camel-endpoint` for component convenience.

Main types: `Component`, `Endpoint`, `Consumer`, `ProducerContext`, `ExchangeEnvelope`, `ComponentBundle`, `PollingConsumer`.
Main modules: `component`, `endpoint`, `consumer`, `producer`, `registrar`.

## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub use endpoint::`- [Endpoint](https://docs.rs/endpoint/trait.Endpoint.html);
- `pub use endpoint::`- [PollingConsumer](https://docs.rs/endpoint/trait.PollingConsumer.html);
- `pub use health_registry::`- [HealthCheckRegistry](https://docs.rs/health_registry/trait.HealthCheckRegistry.html);

- `pub use runtime_observability::`- [RuntimeObservability](https://docs.rs/runtime_observability/trait.RuntimeObservability.html);

# camel_language_rhai - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/camel-language-rhai/0.22.0/camel_language_rhai/

## Expand description

camel-language-rhai — Rhai script language for Camel Rust.

Main types: `RhaiLanguage`, `RhaiExpression`, `RhaiPredicate`, `RhaiMutatingExpression`.
Scripts have access to `body`, `headers`, `header()`, `set_header()`, `property()`, `set_property()`.

[§](https://docs.rs#resource-limits)Resource Limits

Scripts are bounded by configurable limits sourced from `[languages.rhai.limits]`
in `Camel.toml`. When absent, the rust-camel runtime defaults apply:

| Limit | Default |
|---|---|
| `max-operations` | 100,000 |
| `max-string-size` | 1 MiB |
| `max-array-size` | 10,000 elements |
| `max-map-size` | 10,000 entries |
| `max-expression-depth` | 64 |
| `max-function-expression-depth` | 32 |
| `execution-timeout-ms` | 5,000 |

Every limit is `Option<_>`; `None` means “use rust-camel runtime default” (no
default-lie per ADR-0011).

[§](https://docs.rs#covered-threats)Covered threats

- Infinite loops (`loop {}`) — trip`max-operations`and`execution-timeout-ms`(whichever fires first).
- Oversized allocations — strings, arrays, maps each have size caps.
- Pathological nesting — expression and function-expression depths are bounded.

[§](https://docs.rs#timeout-caveat)Timeout caveat

`execution-timeout-ms` wraps `eval_with_scope` in `tokio::time::timeout` +
`spawn_blocking`. When the timeout fires, the route future resolves to an
error, but the blocking thread may continue executing until the script
trips `max-operations` or finishes. This is the same partial-mitigation
caveat shared with the Boa engine.

[§](https://docs.rs#sandboxing)Sandboxing

Rhai scripts **cannot access the host filesystem, network APIs, or Rhai
module loading**. This sandbox is **unconditional** — there is no config
opt-out.

Two structural layers enforce this:

- **Compile time**— the Rhai- `no_module`cargo feature (see root- `Cargo.toml`) disables module loading across the entire crate graph.
- **Runtime**— engines are built via- `Engine::new_raw()`plus an explicit- `StandardPackage`registration. Unlike- `Engine::new()`, this does not install a- `FileModuleResolver`.

Additionally, `eval` and `import` are registered as disabled symbols as
defense in depth (no-op safe if symbols are absent). If a future Rhai
package were to re-introduce module loading or dynamic evaluation, these
symbols would still be blocked to user scripts.

What the sandbox is **not**:

- It is not a CPU/memory cap. Those are separate resource limits; see rc-bpx.
- It does not block timing APIs (`sleep`,`timestamp`). Those remain part of`StandardPackage`; CPU/time-based DoS is covered by rc-bpx resource limits.
- It is not a side-channel defense (cache timing, memory layout). Out of scope.

If your integration genuinely needs filesystem or network access from a
route script, use the explicit Camel components (`file:`, `http:`) with
their own runtime policies — do not attempt to bypass this sandbox.

[§](https://docs.rs#limitations)Limitations

- Resource limits (max operations, string/array/map sizes, expression
depths) are enforced as denial-of-service protection, not as a sandbox.
They are configurable — see [# Resource Limits](https://docs.rs#resource-limits)above.
- The `body`variable is always a string. Structured access to JSON/XML bodies requires explicit parsing within the script using Rhai’s built-in map/array types.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Rhai](https://docs.rs/struct.RhaiLanguage.html)- Language
- Rhai scripting language for rust-camel.

---

# sandogasa_koji - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/sandogasa-koji/0.15.3/sandogasa_koji/

## Expand description

Koji build system CLI wrapper.

Provides functions for querying Koji tags and builds by shelling
out to the `koji` CLI. Supports multiple Koji profiles (e.g.
`cbs` for CentOS Build System).

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [TagAdd](https://docs.rs/struct.TagAddEvent.html)- Event
- One “tagged into” event from `koji list-history --tag=<tag>`. Captures only the bits the activity-reporting code needs; the date column is parsed by the caller as needed.
- [Tagged](https://docs.rs/struct.TaggedBuild.html)- Build
- A build found in a Koji tag.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [build_](https://docs.rs/fn.build_creation_date.html)- creation_ - date
- Parse the build’s creation date from `koji buildinfo`.
- [build_](https://docs.rs/fn.build_info_with_changelog.html)- info_ - with_ - changelog
- Fetch `koji buildinfo --changelog <nvr>`output verbatim for display. Returns the raw stdout so callers can show it to a human reviewing the build. Errors propagate (unlike the date/rpm helpers, an unexpected failure here is worth surfacing during an interactive review).
- [build_](https://docs.rs/fn.build_rpms.html)- rpms
- List binary RPM names for a build via `koji buildinfo`.
- [check_](https://docs.rs/fn.check_auth.html)- auth
- Verify an authenticated Koji session is available for `profile`by running`koji moshimoshi`(the authenticated hello).
- [list_](https://docs.rs/fn.list_tagged.html)- tagged
- List builds in a Koji tag with their owners.
- [list_](https://docs.rs/fn.list_tagged_nvrs.html)- tagged_ - nvrs
- List NVRs in a Koji tag (quiet mode, NVRs only).
- [list_](https://docs.rs/fn.list_tagged_package_names.html)- tagged_ - package_ - names
- List the latest source package names tagged into a Koji tag.
- [list_](https://docs.rs/fn.list_tags.html)- tags
- List Koji tag names matching a glob `pattern`(e.g.`hyperscale10s-*-release`). Wraps`koji list-tags <pattern>`.
- [parse_](https://docs.rs/fn.parse_nvr.html)- nvr
- Parse an NVR string into (name, version, release).
- [parse_](https://docs.rs/fn.parse_nvr_name.html)- nvr_ - name
- Parse an NVR string into the package name.
- [parse_](https://docs.rs/fn.parse_tag_history.html)- tag_ - history
- Parse `koji list-history`output and pick out only the “tagged into” entries. Format of those lines (as of koji 1.34,`--utc`):
- [regen_](https://docs.rs/fn.regen_repo.html)- repo
- Regenerate a Koji tag’s repo (`koji regen-repo --wait <tag>`).
- [tag_](https://docs.rs/fn.tag_build.html)- build
- Tag a build into a Koji tag (`koji tag-build --wait <tag> <nvr>`).
- [tag_](https://docs.rs/fn.tag_history.html)- history
- Walk a tag’s “tagged into” events in the window `[after, before)`and return them in chronological order. Implemented via`koji list-history --tag=<tag>`parsed line-by-line; only`tagged into`lines are kept (other event types like owner changes and untags are filtered out).
- [untag_](https://docs.rs/fn.untag_build.html)- build
- Untag a build from a Koji tag (`koji untag-build <tag> <nvr>`).

# hrdr_tools - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/hrdr-tools/0.2.1/hrdr_tools/

## Expand description

`hrdr-tools` — the agentic tool set.

The locked MVP set: `read_file`, `write_file`, `edit`, `bash`, `grep`,
`glob`, `todo_write`. Each implements [ Tool](https://docs.rs/trait.Tool.html) and is exposed to the model
as a native OpenAI function. Efficiency is in the design: token-bounded
outputs, line-numbered reads for precise edits, ripgrep-backed search.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Bash](https://docs.rs/struct.BashTool.html)- Tool
- [Checkpoint](https://docs.rs/struct.CheckpointInfo.html)- Info
- One revertible checkpoint (a turn that changed files).
- [Checkpoints](https://docs.rs/struct.Checkpoints.html)
- A disk-backed store of per-turn file pre-images.
- [Edit](https://docs.rs/struct.EditTool.html)- Tool
- [Glob](https://docs.rs/struct.GlobTool.html)- Tool
- [Grep](https://docs.rs/struct.GrepTool.html)- Tool
- [Guardrail](https://docs.rs/struct.Guardrail.html)
- One command rule: a regex matched against the whole shell command line and the corrective message returned to the model when it matches.
- [Hook](https://docs.rs/struct.Hook.html)
- One configured hook: run `run`(with`{path}`substituted) after tool`on`successfully mutates a file matching`glob`.
- [Power](https://docs.rs/struct.PowerShellTool.html)- Shell - Tool
- [Read](https://docs.rs/struct.ReadTool.html)- Tool
- [Todo](https://docs.rs/struct.TodoItem.html)- Item
- A single TODO item tracked by `todo_write`.
- [Todo](https://docs.rs/struct.TodoTool.html)- Tool
- [Tool](https://docs.rs/struct.ToolContext.html)- Context
- Shared execution context handed to every tool call.
- [Tool](https://docs.rs/struct.ToolRegistry.html)- Registry
- Ordered registry of tools, keyed by name.
- [WebFetch](https://docs.rs/struct.WebFetchTool.html)- Tool
- [WebSearch](https://docs.rs/struct.WebSearchTool.html)- Tool
- [Write](https://docs.rs/struct.WriteTool.html)- Tool

## Constants[§](https://docs.rs#constants)

- [DEFAULT_](https://docs.rs/constant.DEFAULT_HOOK_TIMEOUT_MS.html)- HOOK_ - TIMEOUT_ - MS
- Default per-hook timeout: formatters are fast; anything slower is stuck.
- [DEFAULT_](https://docs.rs/constant.DEFAULT_MAX_OUTPUT.html)- MAX_ - OUTPUT
- Default cap on a single tool’s textual output, in bytes. Larger results are truncated with a marker so the model’s context is never blown by one call.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Tool](https://docs.rs/trait.Tool.html)
- A model-callable tool.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [available_](https://docs.rs/fn.available_shell_tools.html)- shell_ - tools
- The available shell tools for this machine (bash and/or PowerShell), only
including a tool when its interpreter is actually on `PATH`.
- [cap_](https://docs.rs/fn.cap_matches.html)- matches
- Cap search output at `max_matches`*matches*, appending a count of what was dropped and how to narrow the search. Only`path:NN:…`lines count as matches —`path-NN-…`context lines and`--`group separators (grep/rg`-C`format) ride along with their match, so a context-grep isn’t over-counted.
- [check_](https://docs.rs/fn.check_guardrails.html)- guardrails
- First matching rule’s message, if `command`trips any guardrail. Quoted spans are blanked before matching so string*arguments*that merely mention a blocked command (e.g.`rg 'git add -A'`) don’t false-positive.
- [default_](https://docs.rs/fn.default_guardrails.html)- guardrails
- The built-in rules. Patterns are matched anywhere in the command string
(compound `a && b`commands included). Kept deliberately narrow: they block the exact foot-gun spellings, not whole subcommands.
- [floor_](https://docs.rs/fn.floor_char_boundary.html)- char_ - boundary
- Largest byte index `≤ max`that lies on a UTF-8 char boundary of`s`, so`&s[..floor_char_boundary(s, max)]`never panics on multibyte text. Returns`s.len()`when`max >= s.len()`. (std’s`str::floor_char_boundary`is still unstable, hence this helper.)
- [run_](https://docs.rs/fn.run_file_hooks.html)- file_ - hooks
- Run every hook matching (`tool`,`path`) sequentially, returning one warning line per hook that failed or timed out (empty = all quiet). Success output is discarded — the caller re-reads the file and diffs, so the model sees the effect, not the chatter.
- [truncate](https://docs.rs/fn.truncate.html)
- Truncate `text`to`max`bytes on a char boundary, appending a marker that tells the model output was cut.
- [truncate_](https://docs.rs/fn.truncate_inline.html)- inline
- Collapse `s`to a single line (newlines → spaces) and truncate to`max`**characters**, appending`…`if it was cut. For compact one-line previews (tool-arg previews, status lines) — width-based, unlike the byte-based`truncate`
- [truncate_](https://docs.rs/fn.truncate_middle.html)- middle
- Truncate to `max`bytes keeping the**head and tail**with the omission in the middle. For shell output: build/test runs put the errors at the end, so head-only truncation (plain`truncate`
- [unix_](https://docs.rs/fn.unix_now.html)- now
- Current Unix time in whole seconds (0 if the clock is before the epoch). Shared by checkpoint journaling and session metadata.

- [Release](https://docs.rs/struct.Release.html)
- A GitLab Release as returned by `/projects/:id/releases`. Field selection follows the API’s snake_case names.
- [Release](https://docs.rs/struct.ReleaseAuthor.html)- Author
- Author block on a Release. Username is the field most useful for cross-referencing with the calling user’s profile.
- [Release](https://docs.rs/struct.ReleaseLinks.html)- Links
- `_links`block. The- `self`link is the canonical web URL of the release page.
- [Tag](https://docs.rs/struct.Tag.html)
- A tag as returned by `/projects/:id/repository/tags`. The fields kept here are the ones relevant to an activity-window match: the tag’s`created_at`(when the ref was pushed, distinct from the commit date) and the tag name.
- [User](https://docs.rs/struct.User.html)
- A GitLab user as returned by `/users?username=<name>`.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [count_](https://docs.rs/fn.count_authored_commits.html)- authored_ - commits
- Count commits in `project_id`authored by`author`within`[since, until]`(inclusive). GitLab’s commits endpoint matches the`author`parameter against both name and email fields, so passing the GitLab username usually works; if the user authored commits under an email only, pass that email string instead.
- [list_](https://docs.rs/fn.list_archived_project_names.html)- archived_ - project_ - names
- List the **archived**projects under a GitLab group, returning their names. GitLab’s`archived=true`filter narrows the listing server-side, so this is a cheap separate query rather than enriching every project in the main listing.
- [list_](https://docs.rs/fn.list_group_projects.html)- group_ - projects
- List all projects under a GitLab group (public, no auth needed).
- [list_](https://docs.rs/fn.list_tags.html)- tags
- List tags for a project, paginated. Returns an empty list on
404. Uses `order_by=updated&sort=desc`so newer tags come first — handy when the caller wants to short-circuit on the first tag older than its window of interest.
- [package_](https://docs.rs/fn.package_from_issue_url.html)- from_ - issue_ - url
- Extract the package name from a GitLab issue or work item web_url.
- [parse_](https://docs.rs/fn.parse_issue_url.html)- issue_ - url
- Parse a GitLab issue / work-item URL into its components.
- [parse_](https://docs.rs/fn.parse_mr_url.html)- mr_ - url
- Parse a merge request URL into its components.
- [parse_](https://docs.rs/fn.parse_project_url.html)- project_ - url
- Parse a GitLab project URL into (base_url, project_path).
- [project_](https://docs.rs/fn.project_path_from_issue_url.html)- path_ - from_ - issue_ - url
- Extract the project path from a GitLab issue or work item web_url.
- [project_](https://docs.rs/fn.project_releases.html)- releases
- List releases for a project. Returns an empty list on 404 (project gone) so callers can iterate over many projects without per-project error handling.
- [project_](https://docs.rs/fn.project_summary.html)- summary
- Look up a project’s `path_with_namespace`from its numeric ID. Used to map event`project_id`→ group-prefix filter.
- [user_](https://docs.rs/fn.user_by_username.html)- by_ - username
- Look up a user by username on a specific GitLab instance.
Returns `Ok(None)`if the server returns 200 with an empty list (no user with that name on that instance).
- [user_](https://docs.rs/fn.user_events.html)- events
- Fetch a user’s activity events within `[after, before)`— GitLab’s event endpoint is half-open on both sides and rejects both-null. Results are paginated at 100/page; this follows every page until a short page arrives.
- [validate_](https://docs.rs/fn.validate_token.html)- token
- Check whether a token is valid by calling `GET /api/v4/user`.

# mime_guess2 2.3.1 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/mime_guess2/2.3.1

MIME/MediaType guessing by file extension. Uses a static map of known file extension -> MIME type mappings.

`mime_guess2`is a fork of`mime_guess`([https://github.com/abonander/mime_guess](https://github.com/abonander/mime_guess)), as`mime_guess`is not actively maintained.

**Returning Contributors: New Requirements for Submissions Below**

##### Required Rust Version: 1.85.1

### Versioning

Due to a mistaken premature release, `mime_guess2` currently publicly depends on a pre-1.0 `mime`,
which means `mime` upgrades are breaking changes and necessitate a major version bump.
Refer to the following table to find a version of `mime_guess2` which matches your version of `mime`:

| `mime`version | `mime_guess2`version |
|---|---|
| `0.1.x, 0.2.x` | `1.x.y` |
| `0.3.x` | `2.x.y` |

#### Note: MIME Types Returned Are Not Stable/Guaranteed

The media types returned for a given extension are not considered to be part of the crate's
stable API and are often updated in patch (`x.y.z + 1`) releases to be as correct as possible. MIME
changes are backported to previous major releases on a best-effort basis.

Note that only the extensions of paths/filenames are inspected in order to guess the MIME type. The file that may or may not reside at that path may or may not be a valid file of the returned MIME type. Be wary of unsafe or un-validated assumptions about file structure or length.

An extension may also have multiple applicable MIME types. When more than one is returned, the first is considered to be the most "correct"--see below for elaboration.

## Contributing

#### Adding or correcting MIME types for extensions

Is the MIME type for a file extension wrong or missing? Great! Well, not great for us, but great for you if you'd like to open a pull request!

The file extension -> MIME type mappings are listed in `src/mime_types.rs`.
**The list is sorted lexicographically by file extension, and all extensions are lowercase (where applicable).**
The former is necessary to support fallback to binary search when the
`phf-map` feature is turned off, and for the maintainers' sanity.
The latter is only for consistency's sake; the search is case-insensitive.

Simply add or update the appropriate string pair(s) to make the correction(s) needed.
Run `cargo test` to make sure the library continues to work correctly.

#### Important! Citing the corrected MIME type

When opening a pull request, please include a link to an official document or RFC noting
the correct MIME type for the file type in question **in the commit message** so
that the commit history can be used as an audit trail.

Though we're only guessing here, we like to be as correct as we can. It makes it much easier to vet your contribution if we don't have to search for corroborating material.

#### Multiple MIME types per extension

As of `2.0.0`, multiple MIME types per extension are supported. The first MIME type in the list for
a given extension should be the most "correct" so users who only care about getting a single MIME
type can use the `first*()` methods.

The definition of "correct" is open to debate, however. In the author's opinion this should be whatever is defined by the latest IETF RFC for the given file format, or otherwise explicitly supercedes all others.

If an official IANA registration replaces an older "experimental" style media type, please place the new type before the old type in the list, but keep the old type for reference:

```
- ("md", &["text/x-markdown"]),
+ ("md", &["text/markdown", "text/x-markdown"]),
```
#### Changes to the API or operation of the crate

We're open to changes to the crate's API or its inner workings, breaking or not, if it improves the overall operation, efficiency, or ergonomics of the crate. However, it would be a good idea to open an issue on the repository so we can discuss your proposed changes and decide how best to approach them.

## License

MIT (See the `LICENSE` file in this repository for more information.)

---

# mime_guess2 - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/mime_guess2/2.3.1/target-redirect/mime_guess2/

## Expand description

Guessing of MIME types by file extension.

Uses a static list of file-extension : MIME type mappings.

```
// the file doesn't have to exist, it just looks at the path
let guess = mime_guess2::from_path("some_file.gif");
assert_eq!(guess.first(), Some(mime::IMAGE_GIF));
```
[§](https://docs.rs#note-mime-types-returned-are-not-stableguaranteed)Note: MIME Types Returned Are Not Stable/Guaranteed

The media types returned for a given extension are not considered to be part of the crate’s
stable API and are often updated in patch

 (`x.y.[z + 1]`) releases to be as correct as
possible.

Additionally, only the extensions of paths/filenames are inspected in order to guess the MIME type. The file that may or may not reside at that path may or may not be a valid file of the returned MIME type. Be wary of unsafe or un-validated assumptions about file structure or length.

## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub extern crate`- [mime](https://docs.rs/mime/0.3.17/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/mime/index.html);

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Iter](https://docs.rs/struct.Iter.html)
- An iterator over the `Mime`types of a`MimeGuess`.
- [IterRaw](https://docs.rs/struct.IterRaw.html)
- An iterator over the raw media type strings of a `MimeGuess`.
- [Mime](https://docs.rs/struct.Mime.html)
- A parsed mime or media type.
- [Mime](https://docs.rs/struct.MimeGuess.html)- Guess
- A “guess” of the MIME/Media Type(s) of an extension or path as one or more
`Mime`

[55](https://docs.rs#55)
[56](https://docs.rs#56)impl MimeGuess {
[57](https://docs.rs#57)    /// Guess the MIME type of a file (real or otherwise) with the given extension.
[58](https://docs.rs#58)    ///
[59](https://docs.rs#59)    /// The search is case-insensitive.
[60](https://docs.rs#60)    ///
[61](https://docs.rs#61)    /// If `ext` is empty or has no (currently) known MIME type mapping, then an empty guess is
[62](https://docs.rs#62)    /// returned.
[63](https://docs.rs#63)    pub fn from_ext(ext: &str) -> MimeGuess {
[64](https://docs.rs#64)        if ext.is_empty() {
[65](https://docs.rs#65)            return MimeGuess(&[]);
[66](https://docs.rs#66)        }
[67](https://docs.rs#67)
[68](https://docs.rs#68)        impl_::get_mime_types(ext).map_or(MimeGuess(&[]), |v| MimeGuess(v))
[69](https://docs.rs#69)    }
[70](https://docs.rs#70)
[71](https://docs.rs#71)    /// Guess the MIME type of `path` by its extension (as defined by
[72](https://docs.rs#72)    /// [`Path::extension()`]). **No disk access is performed.**
[73](https://docs.rs#73)    ///
[74](https://docs.rs#74)    /// If `path` has no extension, the extension cannot be converted to `str`, or has
[75](https://docs.rs#75)    /// no known MIME type mapping, then an empty guess is returned.
[76](https://docs.rs#76)    ///
[77](https://docs.rs#77)    /// The search is case-insensitive.
[78](https://docs.rs#78)    ///
[79](https://docs.rs#79)    /// ## Note
[80](https://docs.rs#80)    /// **Guess** is the operative word here, as there are no guarantees that the contents of the
[81](https://docs.rs#81)    /// file that `path` points to match the MIME type associated with the path's extension.
[82](https://docs.rs#82)    ///
[83](https://docs.rs#83)    /// Take care when processing files with assumptions based on the return value of this function.
[84](https://docs.rs#84)    ///
[85](https://docs.rs#85)    /// [`Path::extension()`]: https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/path/struct.Path.html#method.extension
[86](https://docs.rs#86)    pub fn from_path<P: AsRef<Path>>(path: P) -> MimeGuess {
[87](https://docs.rs#87)        path.as_ref()
[88](https://docs.rs#88)            .extension()
[89](https://docs.rs#89)            .and_then(OsStr::to_str)
[90](https://docs.rs#90)            .map_or(MimeGuess(&[]), Self::from_ext)
[91](https://docs.rs#91)    }
[92](https://docs.rs#92)
[93](https://docs.rs#93)    /// `true` if the guess did not return any known mappings for the given path or extension.
[94](https://docs.rs#94)    pub fn is_empty(&self) -> bool {
[95](https://docs.rs#95)        self.0.is_empty()
[96](https://docs.rs#96)    }
[97](https://docs.rs#97)
[98](https://docs.rs#98)    /// Get the number of MIME types in the current guess.
[99](https://docs.rs#99)    pub fn count(&self) -> usize {
[100](https://docs.rs#100)        self.0.len()
[101](https://docs.rs#101)    }
[102](https://docs.rs#102)
[103](https://docs.rs#103)    /// Get the first guessed `Mime`, if applicable.
[104](https://docs.rs#104)    ///
[105](https://docs.rs#105)    /// See [Note: Ordering](#note-ordering) above.
[106](https://docs.rs#106)    pub fn first(&self) -> Option<Mime> {
[107](https://docs.rs#107)        self.first_raw().map(expect_mime)
[108](https://docs.rs#108)    }
[109](https://docs.rs#109)
[110](https://docs.rs#110)    /// Get the first guessed Media Type as a string, if applicable.
[111](https://docs.rs#111)    ///
[112](https://docs.rs#112)    /// See [Note: Ordering](#note-ordering) above.
[113](https://docs.rs#113)    pub fn first_raw(&self) -> Option<&'static str> {
[114](https://docs.rs#114)        self.0.get(0).cloned()
[115](https://docs.rs#115)    }
[116](https://docs.rs#116)
[117](https://docs.rs#117)    /// Get the first guessed `Mime`, or if the guess is empty, return
[118](https://docs.rs#118)    /// [`application/octet-stream`] instead.
[119](https://docs.rs#119)    ///
[120](https://docs.rs#120)    /// See [Note: Ordering](#note-ordering) above.
[121](https://docs.rs#121)    ///
[122](https://docs.rs#122)    /// ### Note: HTTP Applications
[123](https://docs.rs#123)    /// For HTTP request and response bodies if a value for the `Content-Type` header
[124](https://docs.rs#124)    /// cannot be determined it might be preferable to not send one at all instead of defaulting to
[125](https://docs.rs#125)    /// `application/octet-stream` as the recipient will expect to infer the format directly from
[126](https://docs.rs#126)    /// the content instead. ([RFC 7231, Section 3.1.1.5][rfc7231])
[127](https://docs.rs#127)    ///
[128](https://docs.rs#128)    /// On the contrary, for `multipart/form-data` bodies, the `Content-Type` of a form-data part is
[129](https://docs.rs#129)    /// assumed to be `text/plain` unless specified so a default of `application/octet-stream`
[130](https://docs.rs#130)    /// for non-text parts is safer. ([RFC 7578, Section 4.4][rfc7578])
[131](https://docs.rs#131)    ///
[132](https://docs.rs#132)    /// [`application/octet-stream`]: https://docs.rs/mime/0.3/mime/constant.APPLICATION_OCTET_STREAM.html
[133](https://docs.rs#133)    /// [rfc7231]: https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc7231#section-3.1.1.5
[134](https://docs.rs#134)    /// [rfc7578]: https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc7578#section-4.4
[135](https://docs.rs#135)    pub fn first_or_octet_stream(&self) -> Mime {
[136](https://docs.rs#136)        self.first_or(mime::APPLICATION_OCTET_STREAM)
[137](https://docs.rs#137)    }
[138](https://docs.rs#138)
[139](https://docs.rs#139)    /// Get the first guessed `Mime`, or if the guess is empty, return
[140](https://docs.rs#140)    /// [`text/plain`](::mime::TEXT_PLAIN) instead.
[141](https://docs.rs#141)    ///
[142](https://docs.rs#142)    /// See [Note: Ordering](#note-ordering) above.
[143](https://docs.rs#143)    pub fn first_or_text_plain(&self) -> Mime {
[144](https://docs.rs#144)        self.first_or(mime::TEXT_PLAIN)
[145](https://docs.rs#145)    }
[146](https://docs.rs#146)
[147](https://docs.rs#147)    /// Get the first guessed `Mime`, or if the guess is empty, return the given `Mime` instead.
[148](https://docs.rs#148)    ///
[149](https://docs.rs#149)    /// See [Note: Ordering](#note-ordering) above.
[150](https://docs.rs#150)    pub fn first_or(&self, default: Mime) -> Mime {
[151](https://docs.rs#151)        self.first().unwrap_or(default)
[152](https://docs.rs#152)    }
[153](https://docs.rs#153)
[154](https://docs.rs#154)    /// Get the first guessed `Mime`, or if the guess is empty, execute the closure and return its
[155](https://docs.rs#155)    /// result.
[156](https://docs.rs#156)    ///
[157](https://docs.rs#157)    /// See [Note: Ordering](#note-ordering) above.
[158](https://docs.rs#158)    pub fn first_or_else<F>(&self, default_fn: F) -> Mime
[159](https://docs.rs#159)    where
[160](https://docs.rs#160)        F: FnOnce() -> Mime,
[161](https://docs.rs#161)    {
[162](https://docs.rs#162)        self.first().unwrap_or_else(default_fn)
[163](https://docs.rs#163)    }
[164](https://docs.rs#164)
[165](https://docs.rs#165)    /// Get an iterator over the `Mime` values contained in this guess.
[166](https://docs.rs#166)    ///
[167](https://docs.rs#167)    /// See [Note: Ordering](#note-ordering) above.
[168](https://docs.rs#168)    pub fn iter(&self) -> Iter {
[169](https://docs.rs#169)        Iter(self.iter_raw().map(expect_mime))
[170](https://docs.rs#170)    }
[171](https://docs.rs#171)
[172](https://docs.rs#172)    /// Get an iterator over the raw media-type strings in this guess.
[173](https://docs.rs#173)    ///
[174](https://docs.rs#174)    /// See [Note: Ordering](#note-ordering) above.
[175](https://docs.rs#175)    pub fn iter_raw(&self) -> IterRaw {
[176](https://docs.rs#176)        IterRaw(self.0.iter().cloned())
[177](https://docs.rs#177)    }

[278](https://docs.rs#278)/// Guess the MIME type of `path` by its extension (as defined by `Path::extension()`).
[279](https://docs.rs#279)///
[280](https://docs.rs#280)/// If `path` has no extension, or its extension has no known MIME type mapping,
[281](https://docs.rs#281)/// then the MIME type is assumed to be `application/octet-stream`.
[282](https://docs.rs#282)///
[283](https://docs.rs#283)/// ## Note
[284](https://docs.rs#284)/// **Guess** is the operative word here, as there are no guarantees that the contents of the file
[285](https://docs.rs#285)/// that `path` points to match the MIME type associated with the path's extension.
[286](https://docs.rs#286)///
[287](https://docs.rs#287)/// Take care when processing files with assumptions based on the return value of this function.
[288](https://docs.rs#288)///
[289](https://docs.rs#289)/// In HTTP applications, it might be [preferable][rfc7231] to not send a `Content-Type`
[290](https://docs.rs#290)/// header at all instead of defaulting to `application/octet-stream`.
[291](https://docs.rs#291)///
[292](https://docs.rs#292)/// [rfc7231]: https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc7231#section-3.1.1.5
[293](https://docs.rs#293)#[deprecated(
[294](https://docs.rs#294)    since = "2.0.0",
[295](https://docs.rs#295)    note = "Use `from_path(path).first_or_octet_stream()` instead"
[296](https://docs.rs#296))]
[297](https://docs.rs#297)pub fn guess_mime_type<P: AsRef<Path>>(path: P) -> Mime {
[298](https://docs.rs#298)    from_path(path).first_or_octet_stream()
[299](https://docs.rs#299)}
[300](https://docs.rs#300)
[301](https://docs.rs#301)/// Guess the MIME type of `path` by its extension (as defined by `Path::extension()`).
[302](https://docs.rs#302)///
[303](https://docs.rs#303)/// If `path` has no extension, or its extension has no known MIME type mapping,
[304](https://docs.rs#304)/// then `None` is returned.
[305](https://docs.rs#305)///
