[367](https://docs.rs#367)/// Get a list of known extensions for a given `Mime`.
[368](https://docs.rs#368)///
[369](https://docs.rs#369)/// Ignores parameters (only searches with `<main type>/<subtype>`). Case-insensitive (for extension types).
[370](https://docs.rs#370)///
[371](https://docs.rs#371)/// Returns `None` if the MIME type is unknown.
[372](https://docs.rs#372)///
[373](https://docs.rs#373)/// ### Wildcards
[374](https://docs.rs#374)/// If the top-level of the MIME type is a wildcard (`*`), returns all extensions.
[375](https://docs.rs#375)///
[376](https://docs.rs#376)/// If the sub-level of the MIME type is a wildcard, returns all extensions for the top-level.
[377](https://docs.rs#377)#[cfg(feature = "rev-map")]
[378](https://docs.rs#378)pub fn get_mime_extensions(mime: &Mime) -> Option<&'static [&'static str]> {
[379](https://docs.rs#379)    get_extensions(mime.type_().as_ref(), mime.subtype().as_ref())
[380](https://docs.rs#380)}
[381](https://docs.rs#381)
[382](https://docs.rs#382)/// Get a list of known extensions for a MIME type string.
[383](https://docs.rs#383)///
[384](https://docs.rs#384)/// Ignores parameters (only searches `<main type>/<subtype>`). Case-insensitive.
[385](https://docs.rs#385)///
[386](https://docs.rs#386)/// Returns `None` if the MIME type is unknown.
[387](https://docs.rs#387)///
[388](https://docs.rs#388)/// ### Wildcards
[389](https://docs.rs#389)/// If the top-level of the MIME type is a wildcard (`*`), returns all extensions.
[390](https://docs.rs#390)///
[391](https://docs.rs#391)/// If the sub-level of the MIME type is a wildcard, returns all extensions for the top-level.
[392](https://docs.rs#392)///
[393](https://docs.rs#393)/// ### Panics
[394](https://docs.rs#394)/// If `mime_str` is not a valid MIME type specifier (naive).
[395](https://docs.rs#395)#[cfg(feature = "rev-map")]
[396](https://docs.rs#396)pub fn get_mime_extensions_str(mut mime_str: &str) -> Option<&'static [&'static str]> {
[397](https://docs.rs#397)    mime_str = mime_str.trim();
[398](https://docs.rs#398)
[399](https://docs.rs#399)    if let Some(sep_idx) = mime_str.find(';') {
[400](https://docs.rs#400)        mime_str = &mime_str[..sep_idx];
[401](https://docs.rs#401)    }
[402](https://docs.rs#402)
[403](https://docs.rs#403)    let (top, sub) = {
[404](https://docs.rs#404)        let split_idx = mime_str.find('/')?;
[405](https://docs.rs#405)        (&mime_str[..split_idx], &mime_str[split_idx + 1..])
[406](https://docs.rs#406)    };
[407](https://docs.rs#407)
[408](https://docs.rs#408)    get_extensions(top, sub)
[409](https://docs.rs#409)}
[410](https://docs.rs#410)
[411](https://docs.rs#411)/// Get the extensions for a given top-level and sub-level of a MIME type
[412](https://docs.rs#412)/// (`{toplevel}/{sublevel}`).
[413](https://docs.rs#413)///
[414](https://docs.rs#414)/// Returns `None` if `toplevel` or `sublevel` are unknown.
[415](https://docs.rs#415)///
[416](https://docs.rs#416)/// ### Wildcards
[417](https://docs.rs#417)/// If the top-level of the MIME type is a wildcard (`*`), returns all extensions.
[418](https://docs.rs#418)///
[419](https://docs.rs#419)/// If the sub-level of the MIME type is a wildcard, returns all extensions for the top-level.
[420](https://docs.rs#420)#[cfg(feature = "rev-map")]
[421](https://docs.rs#421)pub fn get_extensions(toplevel: &str, sublevel: &str) -> Option<&'static [&'static str]> {
[422](https://docs.rs#422)    impl_::get_extensions(toplevel, sublevel)
[423](https://docs.rs#423)}

[445](https://docs.rs#445)
[446](https://docs.rs#446)        assert_type_bounds::<super::MimeGuess>();

[451](https://docs.rs#451)    #[test]
[452](https://docs.rs#452)    fn test_mime_type_guessing() {
[453](https://docs.rs#453)        assert_eq!(
[454](https://docs.rs#454)            from_ext("gif").first_or_octet_stream().to_string(),
[455](https://docs.rs#455)            "image/gif".to_string()
[456](https://docs.rs#456)        );
[457](https://docs.rs#457)        assert_eq!(
[458](https://docs.rs#458)            from_ext("TXT").first_or_octet_stream().to_string(),
[459](https://docs.rs#459)            "text/plain".to_string()
[460](https://docs.rs#460)        );
[461](https://docs.rs#461)        assert_eq!(
[462](https://docs.rs#462)            from_ext("blahblah").first_or_octet_stream().to_string(),
[463](https://docs.rs#463)            "application/octet-stream".to_string()
[464](https://docs.rs#464)        );
[465](https://docs.rs#465)
[466](https://docs.rs#466)        assert_eq!(
[467](https://docs.rs#467)            from_path(Path::new("/path/to/file.gif"))
[468](https://docs.rs#468)                .first_or_octet_stream()
[469](https://docs.rs#469)                .to_string(),
[470](https://docs.rs#470)            "image/gif".to_string()
[471](https://docs.rs#471)        );
[472](https://docs.rs#472)        assert_eq!(
[473](https://docs.rs#473)            from_path("/path/to/file.gif")
[474](https://docs.rs#474)                .first_or_octet_stream()
[475](https://docs.rs#475)                .to_string(),
[476](https://docs.rs#476)            "image/gif".to_string()
[477](https://docs.rs#477)        );
[478](https://docs.rs#478)    }
[479](https://docs.rs#479)
[480](https://docs.rs#480)    #[test]
[481](https://docs.rs#481)    fn test_mime_type_guessing_opt() {
[482](https://docs.rs#482)        assert_eq!(
[483](https://docs.rs#483)            from_ext("gif").first().unwrap().to_string(),
[484](https://docs.rs#484)            "image/gif".to_string()
[485](https://docs.rs#485)        );
[486](https://docs.rs#486)        assert_eq!(
[487](https://docs.rs#487)            from_ext("TXT").first().unwrap().to_string(),
[488](https://docs.rs#488)            "text/plain".to_string()
[489](https://docs.rs#489)        );
[490](https://docs.rs#490)        assert_eq!(from_ext("blahblah").first(), None);
[491](https://docs.rs#491)
[492](https://docs.rs#492)        assert_eq!(
[493](https://docs.rs#493)            from_path("/path/to/file.gif").first().unwrap().to_string(),
[494](https://docs.rs#494)            "image/gif".to_string()
[495](https://docs.rs#495)        );
[496](https://docs.rs#496)        assert_eq!(from_path("/path/to/file").first(), None);
[497](https://docs.rs#497)    }
[498](https://docs.rs#498)
[499](https://docs.rs#499)    #[test]
[500](https://docs.rs#500)    fn test_are_mime_types_parseable() {
[501](https://docs.rs#501)        for (_, mimes) in MIME_TYPES {
[502](https://docs.rs#502)            mimes.iter().for_each(|s| {
[503](https://docs.rs#503)                expect_mime(s);
[504](https://docs.rs#504)            });
[505](https://docs.rs#505)        }
[506](https://docs.rs#506)    }

[510](https://docs.rs#510)    fn test_are_extensions_ascii() {
[511](https://docs.rs#511)        for (ext, _) in MIME_TYPES {
[512](https://docs.rs#512)            assert!(ext.is_ascii(), "Extension not ASCII: {:?}", ext);
[513](https://docs.rs#513)        }
[514](https://docs.rs#514)    }
[515](https://docs.rs#515)
[516](https://docs.rs#516)    #[test]
[517](https://docs.rs#517)    fn test_are_extensions_sorted() {
[518](https://docs.rs#518)        // simultaneously checks the requirement that duplicate extension entries are adjacent
[519](https://docs.rs#519)        for (&(ext, _), &(n_ext, _)) in MIME_TYPES.iter().zip(MIME_TYPES.iter().skip(1)) {
[520](https://docs.rs#520)            assert!(
[521](https://docs.rs#521)                ext <= n_ext,
[522](https://docs.rs#522)                "Extensions in src/mime_types should be sorted lexicographically
[523](https://docs.rs#523)                in ascending order. Failed assert: {:?} <= {:?}",
[524](https://docs.rs#524)                ext,
[525](https://docs.rs#525)                n_ext
[526](https://docs.rs#526)            );
[527](https://docs.rs#527)        }
[528](https://docs.rs#528)    }
[529](https://docs.rs#529)

# Mime in mime_guess2 - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/mime_guess2/2.3.1/mime_guess2/struct.Mime.html

`pub struct Mime { /* private fields */ }`## Expand description

A parsed mime or media type.

## Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#implementations)

Get an optional +suffix for this `Mime`.

[§](https://docs.rs#example-2)Example

```
let svg = "image/svg+xml".parse::<mime::Mime>().unwrap();
assert_eq!(svg.suffix(), Some(mime::XML));
assert_eq!(svg.suffix().unwrap(), "xml");
assert!(mime::TEXT_PLAIN.suffix().is_none());
```
Look up a parameter by name.

[§](https://docs.rs#example-3)Example

```
let mime = mime::TEXT_PLAIN_UTF_8;
assert_eq!(mime.get_param(mime::CHARSET), Some(mime::UTF_8));
assert_eq!(mime.get_param("charset").unwrap(), "utf-8");
assert!(mime.get_param("boundary").is_none());
let mime = "multipart/form-data; boundary=ABCDEFG".parse::<mime::Mime>().unwrap();
assert_eq!(mime.get_param(mime::BOUNDARY).unwrap(), "ABCDEFG");
```

# MimeGuess in mime_guess2 - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/mime_guess2/2.3.1/mime_guess2/struct.MimeGuess.html

`pub struct MimeGuess(/* private fields */);`## Expand description

A “guess” of the MIME/Media Type(s) of an extension or path as one or more
[ Mime](https://docs.rs/struct.Mime.html) instances.

[§](https://docs.rs#note-ordering)Note: Ordering

A given file format may have one or more applicable Media Types; in this case the first Media Type returned is whatever is declared in the latest IETF RFC for the presumed file format or the one that explicitly supercedes all others. Ordering of additional Media Types is arbitrary.

[§](https://docs.rs#note-values-not-stable)Note: Values Not Stable

The exact Media Types returned in any given guess are not considered to be stable and are often updated in patch releases in order to reflect the most up-to-date information possible.

## Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#implementations)

Guess the MIME type of a file (real or otherwise) with the given extension.

The search is case-insensitive.

If `ext` is empty or has no (currently) known MIME type mapping, then an empty guess is
returned.

Guess the MIME type of `path` by its extension (as defined by
[ Path::extension()](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/path/struct.Path.html#method.extension)).

**No disk access is performed.**

If `path` has no extension, the extension cannot be converted to `str`, or has
no known MIME type mapping, then an empty guess is returned.

The search is case-insensitive.

[§](https://docs.rs#note)Note

**Guess** is the operative word here, as there are no guarantees that the contents of the
file that `path` points to match the MIME type associated with the path’s extension.

Take care when processing files with assumptions based on the return value of this function.

`true` if the guess did not return any known mappings for the given path or extension.

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/mime_guess2/lib.rs.html#135-137)#### pub fn [first_or_octet_stream](https://docs.rs#method.first_or_octet_stream)(&self) -> [Mime](https://docs.rs/struct.Mime.html)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/mime_guess2/lib.rs.html#135-137)

#### pub fn [first_or_octet_stream](https://docs.rs#method.first_or_octet_stream)(&self) -> [Mime](https://docs.rs/struct.Mime.html)

Get the first guessed `Mime`, or if the guess is empty, return
[ application/octet-stream](https://docs.rs/mime/0.3/mime/constant.APPLICATION_OCTET_STREAM.html) instead.

See [Note: Ordering](https://docs.rs#note-ordering) above.

[§](https://docs.rs#note-http-applications)Note: HTTP Applications

For HTTP request and response bodies if a value for the `Content-Type` header
cannot be determined it might be preferable to not send one at all instead of defaulting to
`application/octet-stream` as the recipient will expect to infer the format directly from
the content instead. ([RFC 7231, Section 3.1.1.5](https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc7231#section-3.1.1.5))

On the contrary, for `multipart/form-data` bodies, the `Content-Type` of a form-data part is
assumed to be `text/plain` unless specified so a default of `application/octet-stream`
for non-text parts is safer. ([RFC 7578, Section 4.4](https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc7578#section-4.4))

# get_extensions in mime_guess2 - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/mime_guess2/2.3.1/mime_guess2/fn.get_extensions.html

## Expand description

Get the extensions for a given top-level and sub-level of a MIME type
(`{toplevel}/{sublevel}`).

Returns `None` if `toplevel` or `sublevel` are unknown.

[§](https://docs.rs#wildcards)Wildcards

If the top-level of the MIME type is a wildcard (`*`), returns all extensions.

If the sub-level of the MIME type is a wildcard, returns all extensions for the top-level.

# guess_mime_type in mime_guess2 - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/mime_guess2/2.3.1/mime_guess2/fn.guess_mime_type.html

Use `from_path(path).first_or_octet_stream()` instead

## Expand description

Guess the MIME type of `path` by its extension (as defined by `Path::extension()`).

If `path` has no extension, or its extension has no known MIME type mapping,
then the MIME type is assumed to be `application/octet-stream`.

[§](https://docs.rs#note)Note

**Guess** is the operative word here, as there are no guarantees that the contents of the file
that `path` points to match the MIME type associated with the path’s extension.

Take care when processing files with assumptions based on the return value of this function.

In HTTP applications, it might be [preferable](https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc7231#section-3.1.1.5) to not send a `Content-Type`
header at all instead of defaulting to `application/octet-stream`.

# mime_guess2 - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/mime_guess2/latest/mime_guess2/

## Expand description

Guessing of MIME types by file extension.

Uses a static list of file-extension : MIME type mappings.

```
// the file doesn't have to exist, it just looks at the path
let guess = mime_guess2::from_path("some_file.gif");
assert_eq!(guess.first(), Some(mime::IMAGE_GIF));
```
[§](https://docs.rs#note-mime-types-returned-are-not-stableguaranteed)Note: MIME Types Returned Are Not Stable/Guaranteed

The media types returned for a given extension are not considered to be part of the crate’s
stable API and are often updated in patch

 (`x.y.[z + 1]`) releases to be as correct as
possible.

Additionally, only the extensions of paths/filenames are inspected in order to guess the MIME type. The file that may or may not reside at that path may or may not be a valid file of the returned MIME type. Be wary of unsafe or un-validated assumptions about file structure or length.

## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

# mime 0.3.17 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/mime/^0.3

# mime

Support MIME (Media Types) as strong types in Rust.

## Usage

```
extern crate mime;
// common types are constants
let text = TEXT_PLAIN;
// deconstruct Mimes to match on them
match
```
Support MIME (Media Types) as strong types in Rust.

```
extern crate mime;
// common types are constants
let text = mime::TEXT_PLAIN;
// deconstruct Mimes to match on them
match (text.type_(), text.subtype()) {
    (mime::TEXT, mime::PLAIN) => {
        // plain text!
    },
    (mime::TEXT, _) => {
        // structured text!
    },
    _ => {
        // not text!
    }
}
```

---

# phf 0.11.3 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/phf/^0.11

# Rust-PHF

Rust-PHF is a library to generate efficient lookup tables at compile time using
[perfect hash functions](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perfect_hash_function).

It currently uses the
[CHD algorithm](http://cmph.sourceforge.net/papers/esa09.pdf) and can generate
a 100,000 entry map in roughly .4 seconds.

MSRV (minimum supported rust version) is Rust 1.61.

## Usage

PHF data structures can be constructed via either the procedural
macros in the `phf_macros` crate or code generation supported by the
`phf_codegen` crate.

To compile the `phf` crate with a dependency on
libcore instead of libstd, enabling use in environments where libstd
will not work, set `default-features = false` for the dependency:

```
[]
# to use `phf` in `no_std` environments
 = {  = "0.11",  = false }
```
### phf_macros

```
use phf_map;
static KEYWORDS: Map = phf_map! ;
```
```
[]
 = {  = "0.11",  = ["macros"] }
```
#### Note

Currently, the macro syntax has some limitations and may not
work as you want. See [#183](https://github.com/rust-phf/rust-phf/issues/183) or [#196](https://github.com/rust-phf/rust-phf/issues/196) for example.

### phf_codegen

To use `phf_codegen` on build.rs, you have to add dependencies under `[build-dependencies]`:

```
[]
 = {  = "0.11.1",  = false }
 = "0.11.1"
```
Then put code on build.rs:

```
use env;
use File;
use ;
use Path;
```
and lib.rs:

```
include!;
```

# unicase 2.9.0 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/unicase/^2.8.1

# unicase

Compare strings when case is not important (using Unicode Case-folding).

```
// ignore ASCII case
let a = new;
let b = new;
assert_eq!;
// using unicode case-folding
let c = new
let d = new;
assert_eq!;
```

# divan 0.1.21 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/divan/^0.1.17

## Sponsor

If you or your company find Divan valuable, consider [sponsoring on
GitHub](https://github.com/sponsors/nvzqz) or [donating via
PayPal](https://paypal.me/nvzqz). Sponsorships help me progress on what's
possible with benchmarking in Rust.

## Guide

A guide is being worked on. In the meantime, see:

## Getting Started

Divan `0.1.21` requires Rust `1.80.0` or later.

-
Add the following to your project's `Cargo.toml``[] = "0.1.21" [[]] = "example" = false`
-
Create a benchmarks file at `benches/example.rs`[^1] with your benchmarking code:`// Register a `fibonacci` function and benchmark it over multiple cases.`
-
Run your benchmarks with `cargo bench``example fastest │ slowest │ median │ mean │ samples │ iters ╰─ fibonacci │ │ │ │ │ ├─ 1 0.626 ns │ 1.735 ns │ 0.657 ns │ 0.672 ns │ 100 │ 819200 ├─ 2 2.767 ns │ 3.154 ns │ 2.788 ns │ 2.851 ns │ 100 │ 204800 ├─ 4 6.816 ns │ 7.671 ns │ 7.061 ns │ 7.167 ns │ 100 │ 102400 ├─ 8 57.31 ns │ 62.51 ns │ 57.96 ns │ 58.55 ns │ 100 │ 12800 ├─ 16 2.874 µs │ 3.812 µs │ 2.916 µs │ 3.006 µs │ 100 │ 200 ╰─ 32 6.267 ms │ 6.954 ms │ 6.283 ms │ 6.344 ms │ 100 │ 100`

See [ #[divan::bench]](https://docs.rs/divan/latest/divan/attr.bench.html) for info on benchmark function registration.

## Examples

Practical example benchmarks can be found in the [ examples/benches](https://github.com/nvzqz/divan/tree/main/examples/benches)
directory. These can be benchmarked locally by running:

```
```
More thorough usage examples can be found in the [ #[divan::bench] documentation](https://docs.rs/divan/latest/divan/attr.bench.html#examples).

# phf_codegen 0.11.3 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/phf_codegen/^0.11

# Rust-PHF

Rust-PHF is a library to generate efficient lookup tables at compile time using
[perfect hash functions](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perfect_hash_function).

It currently uses the
[CHD algorithm](http://cmph.sourceforge.net/papers/esa09.pdf) and can generate
a 100,000 entry map in roughly .4 seconds.

MSRV (minimum supported rust version) is Rust 1.61.

## Usage

PHF data structures can be constructed via either the procedural
macros in the `phf_macros` crate or code generation supported by the
`phf_codegen` crate.

To compile the `phf` crate with a dependency on
libcore instead of libstd, enabling use in environments where libstd
will not work, set `default-features = false` for the dependency:

```
[]
# to use `phf` in `no_std` environments
 = {  = "0.11",  = false }
```
### phf_macros

```
use phf_map;
static KEYWORDS: Map = phf_map! ;
```
```
[]
 = {  = "0.11",  = ["macros"] }
```
#### Note

Currently, the macro syntax has some limitations and may not
work as you want. See [#183](https://github.com/rust-phf/rust-phf/issues/183) or [#196](https://github.com/rust-phf/rust-phf/issues/196) for example.

### phf_codegen

To use `phf_codegen` on build.rs, you have to add dependencies under `[build-dependencies]`:

```
[]
 = {  = "0.11.1",  = false }
 = "0.11.1"
```
Then put code on build.rs:

```
use env;
use File;
use ;
use Path;
```
and lib.rs:

```
include!;
```

# mime_guess2 2.3.0 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/mime_guess2/2.3.0

MIME/MediaType guessing by file extension. Uses a static map of known file extension -> MIME type mappings.

**Returning Contributors: New Requirements for Submissions Below**

##### Required Rust Version: 1.85.1

### Versioning

Due to a mistaken premature release, `mime_guess2` currently publicly depends on a pre-1.0 `mime`,
which means `mime` upgrades are breaking changes and necessitate a major version bump.
Refer to the following table to find a version of `mime_guess2` which matches your version of `mime`:

| `mime`version | `mime_guess2`version |
|---|---|
| `0.1.x, 0.2.x` | `1.x.y` |
| `0.3.x` | `2.x.y` |

#### Note: MIME Types Returned Are Not Stable/Guaranteed

The media types returned for a given extension are not considered to be part of the crate's
stable API and are often updated in patch (`x.y.z + 1`) releases to be as correct as possible. MIME
changes are backported to previous major releases on a best-effort basis.

Note that only the extensions of paths/filenames are inspected in order to guess the MIME type. The file that may or may not reside at that path may or may not be a valid file of the returned MIME type. Be wary of unsafe or un-validated assumptions about file structure or length.

An extension may also have multiple applicable MIME types. When more than one is returned, the first is considered to be the most "correct"--see below for elaboration.

## Contributing

#### Adding or correcting MIME types for extensions

Is the MIME type for a file extension wrong or missing? Great! Well, not great for us, but great for you if you'd like to open a pull request!

The file extension -> MIME type mappings are listed in `src/mime_types.rs`.
**The list is sorted lexicographically by file extension, and all extensions are lowercase (where applicable).**
The former is necessary to support fallback to binary search when the
`phf-map` feature is turned off, and for the maintainers' sanity.
The latter is only for consistency's sake; the search is case-insensitive.

Simply add or update the appropriate string pair(s) to make the correction(s) needed.
Run `cargo test` to make sure the library continues to work correctly.

#### Important! Citing the corrected MIME type

When opening a pull request, please include a link to an official document or RFC noting
the correct MIME type for the file type in question **in the commit message** so
that the commit history can be used as an audit trail.

Though we're only guessing here, we like to be as correct as we can. It makes it much easier to vet your contribution if we don't have to search for corroborating material.

#### Multiple MIME types per extension

As of `2.0.0`, multiple MIME types per extension are supported. The first MIME type in the list for
a given extension should be the most "correct" so users who only care about getting a single MIME
type can use the `first*()` methods.

The definition of "correct" is open to debate, however. In the author's opinion this should be whatever is defined by the latest IETF RFC for the given file format, or otherwise explicitly supercedes all others.

If an official IANA registration replaces an older "experimental" style media type, please place the new type before the old type in the list, but keep the old type for reference:

```
- ("md", &["text/x-markdown"]),
+ ("md", &["text/markdown", "text/x-markdown"]),
```
#### Changes to the API or operation of the crate

We're open to changes to the crate's API or its inner workings, breaking or not, if it improves the overall operation, efficiency, or ergonomics of the crate. However, it would be a good idea to open an issue on the repository so we can discuss your proposed changes and decide how best to approach them.

## License

MIT (See the `LICENSE` file in this repository for more information.)

---

# mime_guess2 2.3.1 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/mime_guess2/latest/source/README.md

```
MIME/MediaType guessing by file extension.
Uses a static map of known file extension -> MIME type mappings.
**Returning Contributors: New Requirements for Submissions Below**
Due to a mistaken premature release, `mime_guess2` currently publicly depends on a pre-1.0 `mime`,
which means `mime` upgrades are breaking changes and necessitate a major version bump.
Refer to the following table to find a version of `mime_guess2` which matches your version of `mime`:
The media types returned for a given extension are not considered to be part of the crate's
 stable API and are often updated in patch (`x.y.z + 1`) releases to be as correct as possible. MIME
 changes are backported to previous major releases on a best-effort basis.

Note that only the extensions of paths/filenames are inspected in order to guess the MIME type. The
file that may or may not reside at that path may or may not be a valid file of the returned MIME type.
Be wary of unsafe or un-validated assumptions about file structure or length.
An extension may also have multiple applicable MIME types. When more than one is returned, the first
is considered to be the most "correct"--see below for elaboration.
Contributing
Is the MIME type for a file extension wrong or missing? Great!
Well, not great for us, but great for you if you'd like to open a pull request!
The file extension -> MIME type mappings are listed in `src/mime_types.rs`.
**The list is sorted lexicographically by file extension, and all extensions are lowercase (where applicable).**
The former is necessary to support fallback to binary search when the
`phf-map` feature is turned off, and for the maintainers' sanity.
The latter is only for consistency's sake; the search is case-insensitive.
Simply add or update the appropriate string pair(s) to make the correction(s) needed.
Run `cargo test` to make sure the library continues to work correctly.
When opening a pull request, please include a link to an official document or RFC noting
the correct MIME type for the file type in question **in the commit message** so
that the commit history can be used as an audit trail.
Though we're only guessing here, we like to be as correct as we can.
It makes it much easier to vet your contribution if we don't have to search for corroborating material.
As of `2.0.0`, multiple MIME types per extension are supported. The first MIME type in the list for
a given extension should be the most "correct" so users who only care about getting a single MIME
type can use the `first*()` methods.
The definition of "correct" is open to debate, however. In the author's opinion this should be
whatever is defined by the latest IETF RFC for the given file format, or otherwise explicitly
supercedes all others.
If an official IANA registration replaces an older "experimental" style media type, please
place the new type before the old type in the list, but keep the old type for reference:
```
- +
```

# mime 0.3.17 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/mime/0.3.17

# mime

Support MIME (Media Types) as strong types in Rust.

## Usage

```
extern crate mime;
// common types are constants
let text = TEXT_PLAIN;
// deconstruct Mimes to match on them
match
```
Support MIME (Media Types) as strong types in Rust.

```
extern crate mime;
// common types are constants
let text = mime::TEXT_PLAIN;
// deconstruct Mimes to match on them
match (text.type_(), text.subtype()) {
    (mime::TEXT, mime::PLAIN) => {
        // plain text!
    },
    (mime::TEXT, _) => {
        // structured text!
    },
    _ => {
        // not text!
    }
}
```

# mime - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/mime/0.3.17/target-redirect/mime/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#mime)Mime

Mime is now Media Type, technically, but `Mime` is more immediately
understandable, so the main type here is `Mime`.

[§](https://docs.rs#what-is-mime)What is Mime?

Example mime string: `text/plain`

```
let plain_text: mime::Mime = "text/plain".parse().unwrap();
assert_eq!(plain_text, mime::TEXT_PLAIN);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#inspecting-mimes)Inspecting Mimes

```
let mime = mime::TEXT_PLAIN;
match (mime.type_(), mime.subtype()) {
    (mime::TEXT, mime::PLAIN) => println!("plain text!"),
    (mime::TEXT, _) => println!("structured text"),
    _ => println!("not text"),
}
```
## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [From](https://docs.rs/struct.FromStrError.html)- StrError
- An error when parsing a `Mime`from a string.
- [Mime](https://docs.rs/struct.Mime.html)
- A parsed mime or media type.
- [Mime](https://docs.rs/struct.MimeIter.html)- Iter
- An iterator of parsed mime
- [Name](https://docs.rs/struct.Name.html)
- A section of a `Mime`.
- [Params](https://docs.rs/struct.Params.html)
- An iterator over the parameters of a MIME.

# Mime in mime - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/mime/^0.3/struct.Mime.html

`pub struct Mime { /* private fields */ }`## Expand description

A parsed mime or media type.

## Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#implementations)

Get an optional +suffix for this `Mime`.

[§](https://docs.rs#example-2)Example

```
let svg = "image/svg+xml".parse::<mime::Mime>().unwrap();
assert_eq!(svg.suffix(), Some(mime::XML));
assert_eq!(svg.suffix().unwrap(), "xml");
assert!(mime::TEXT_PLAIN.suffix().is_none());
```
Look up a parameter by name.

[§](https://docs.rs#example-3)Example

```
let mime = mime::TEXT_PLAIN_UTF_8;
assert_eq!(mime.get_param(mime::CHARSET), Some(mime::UTF_8));
assert_eq!(mime.get_param("charset").unwrap(), "utf-8");
assert!(mime.get_param("boundary").is_none());
let mime = "multipart/form-data; boundary=ABCDEFG".parse::<mime::Mime>().unwrap();
assert_eq!(mime.get_param(mime::BOUNDARY).unwrap(), "ABCDEFG");
```
## Trait Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#trait-implementations)

# Name in mime - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/mime/^0.3/struct.Name.html

`pub struct Name<'a> { /* private fields */ }`## Expand description

A section of a `Mime`.

For instance, for the Mime `image/svg+xml`, it contains 3 `Name`s,
`image`, `svg`, and `xml`.

In most cases, `Name`s are compared ignoring case.

## Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#implementations)

Get the value of this `Name` as a string.

Note that the borrow is not tied to `&self` but the `'a` lifetime, allowing the
string to outlive `Name`. Alternately, there is an `impl<'a> From<Name<'a>> for &'a str`
which isn’t rendered by Rustdoc, that can be accessed using `str::from(name)` or `name.into()`.

## Trait Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#trait-implementations)

# phf 0.11.3 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/phf/0.11.3

# Rust-PHF

Rust-PHF is a library to generate efficient lookup tables at compile time using
[perfect hash functions](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perfect_hash_function).

It currently uses the
[CHD algorithm](http://cmph.sourceforge.net/papers/esa09.pdf) and can generate
a 100,000 entry map in roughly .4 seconds.

MSRV (minimum supported rust version) is Rust 1.61.

## Usage

PHF data structures can be constructed via either the procedural
macros in the `phf_macros` crate or code generation supported by the
`phf_codegen` crate.

To compile the `phf` crate with a dependency on
libcore instead of libstd, enabling use in environments where libstd
will not work, set `default-features = false` for the dependency:

```
[]
# to use `phf` in `no_std` environments
 = {  = "0.11",  = false }
```
### phf_macros

```
use phf_map;
static KEYWORDS: Map = phf_map! ;
```
```
[]
 = {  = "0.11",  = ["macros"] }
```
#### Note

Currently, the macro syntax has some limitations and may not
work as you want. See [#183](https://github.com/rust-phf/rust-phf/issues/183) or [#196](https://github.com/rust-phf/rust-phf/issues/196) for example.

### phf_codegen

To use `phf_codegen` on build.rs, you have to add dependencies under `[build-dependencies]`:

```
[]
 = {  = "0.11.1",  = false }
 = "0.11.1"
```
Then put code on build.rs:

```
use env;
use File;
use ;
use Path;
```
and lib.rs:

```
include!;
```

---

# Crate phf_macrosCopy item path

[Source](../src/phf_macros/lib.rs.html#1-338)

Expand description

A set of macros to generate Rust source for PHF data structures at compile time. See [the `phf` crate’s documentation](https://docs.rs/phf) for details.

# serde - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/serde/^1.0/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#serde)Serde

Serde is a framework for * ser*ializing and

*serializing Rust data structures efficiently and generically.*

**de**The Serde ecosystem consists of data structures that know how to serialize and deserialize themselves along with data formats that know how to serialize and deserialize other things. Serde provides the layer by which these two groups interact with each other, allowing any supported data structure to be serialized and deserialized using any supported data format.

See the Serde website [https://serde.rs](https://serde.rs) for additional documentation and
usage examples.

[§](https://docs.rs#design)Design

Where many other languages rely on runtime reflection for serializing data,
Serde is instead built on Rust’s powerful trait system. A data structure
that knows how to serialize and deserialize itself is one that implements
Serde’s `Serialize` and `Deserialize` traits (or uses Serde’s derive
attribute to automatically generate implementations at compile time). This
avoids any overhead of reflection or runtime type information. In fact in
many situations the interaction between data structure and data format can
be completely optimized away by the Rust compiler, leaving Serde
serialization to perform the same speed as a handwritten serializer for the
specific selection of data structure and data format.

[§](https://docs.rs#data-formats)Data formats

The following is a partial list of data formats that have been implemented for Serde by the community.

- [JSON](https://github.com/serde-rs/json), the ubiquitous JavaScript Object Notation used by many HTTP APIs.
- [Postcard](https://github.com/jamesmunns/postcard), a no_std and embedded-systems friendly compact binary format.
- [CBOR](https://github.com/enarx/ciborium), a Concise Binary Object Representation designed for small message size without the need for version negotiation.
- [YAML](https://github.com/dtolnay/serde-yaml), a self-proclaimed human-friendly configuration language that ain’t markup language.
- [MessagePack](https://github.com/3Hren/msgpack-rust), an efficient binary format that resembles a compact JSON.
- [TOML](https://docs.rs/toml), a minimal configuration format used by- [Cargo](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/manifest.html).
- [Pickle](https://github.com/birkenfeld/serde-pickle), a format common in the Python world.
- [RON](https://github.com/ron-rs/ron), a Rusty Object Notation.
- [BSON](https://github.com/mongodb/bson-rust), the data storage and network transfer format used by MongoDB.
- [Avro](https://docs.rs/apache-avro), a binary format used within Apache Hadoop, with support for schema definition.
- [JSON5](https://github.com/callum-oakley/json5-rs), a superset of JSON including some productions from ES5.
- [URL](https://docs.rs/serde_qs)query strings, in the x-www-form-urlencoded format.
- [Starlark](https://github.com/dtolnay/serde-starlark), the format used for describing build targets by the Bazel and Buck build systems.- *(serialization only)*
- [Envy](https://github.com/softprops/envy), a way to deserialize environment variables into Rust structs.- *(deserialization only)*
- [Envy Store](https://github.com/softprops/envy-store), a way to deserialize- [AWS Parameter Store](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/systems-manager/latest/userguide/systems-manager-parameter-store.html)parameters into Rust structs.- *(deserialization only)*
- [S-expressions](https://github.com/rotty/lexpr-rs), the textual representation of code and data used by the Lisp language family.
- [D-Bus](https://docs.rs/zvariant)’s binary wire format.
- [FlexBuffers](https://github.com/google/flatbuffers/tree/master/rust/flexbuffers), the schemaless cousin of Google’s FlatBuffers zero-copy serialization format.
- [Bencode](https://github.com/P3KI/bendy), a simple binary format used in the BitTorrent protocol.
- [Token streams](https://github.com/oxidecomputer/serde_tokenstream), for processing Rust procedural macro input.- *(deserialization only)*
- [DynamoDB Items](https://docs.rs/serde_dynamo), the format used by- [rusoto_dynamodb](https://docs.rs/rusoto_dynamodb)to transfer data to and from DynamoDB.
- [Hjson](https://github.com/Canop/deser-hjson), a syntax extension to JSON designed around human reading and editing.- *(deserialization only)*
- [CSV](https://docs.rs/csv), Comma-separated values is a tabular text file format.

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [de](https://docs.rs/de/index.html)
- Generic data structure deserialization framework.
- [ser](https://docs.rs/ser/index.html)
- Generic data structure serialization framework.

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [forward_](https://docs.rs/macro.forward_to_deserialize_any.html)- to_ - deserialize_ - any - `docsrs`
- Helper macro when implementing the `Deserializer`part of a new data format for Serde.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Deserialize](https://docs.rs/trait.Deserialize.html)
- A **data structure**that can be deserialized from any data format supported by Serde.
- [Deserializer](https://docs.rs/trait.Deserializer.html)
- A **data format**that can deserialize any data structure supported by Serde.
- [Serialize](https://docs.rs/trait.Serialize.html)
- A **data structure**that can be serialized into any data format supported by Serde.
- [Serializer](https://docs.rs/trait.Serializer.html)
- A **data format**that can serialize any data structure supported by Serde.

## Derive Macros[§](https://docs.rs#derives)

- [Deserialize](https://docs.rs/derive.Deserialize.html)- `derive`
- Derive macro available if serde is built with `features = ["derive"]`.
- [Serialize](https://docs.rs/derive.Serialize.html)- `derive`
- Derive macro available if serde is built with `features = ["derive"]`.

# phf - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/phf/latest/target-redirect/phf/

## Expand description

Rust-PHF is a library to generate efficient lookup tables at compile time using
[perfect hash functions](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perfect_hash_function).

It currently uses the
[CHD algorithm](http://cmph.sourceforge.net/papers/esa09.pdf) by default and
also ships an experimental `ptrhash` feature for an alternative MPHF layout.

MSRV (minimum supported rust version) is Rust 1.85.

[§](https://docs.rs#usage)Usage

PHF data structures can be constructed via either the procedural
macros in the `phf_macros` crate or code generation supported by the
`phf_codegen` crate. If you prefer macros, you can easily use them by
enabling the `macros` feature of the `phf` crate, like:

```
 [dependencies]
 phf = { version = "0.14.0", features = ["macros"] }
```
To try the experimental MPHF alternative instead of the default CHD layout,
enable the `ptrhash` feature on every `phf` crate involved in generation and
runtime lookup:

```
[dependencies]
phf = { version = "0.14.0", features = ["macros", "ptrhash"] }
```
To compile the `phf` crate with a dependency on
libcore instead of libstd, enabling use in environments where libstd
will not work, set `default-features = false` for the dependency:

```
[dependencies]
# to use `phf` in `no_std` environments
phf = { version = "0.14.0", default-features = false }
```
[§](https://docs.rs#example-with-the-macros-feature-enabled)Example (with the `macros` feature enabled)

```
use phf::phf_map;
#[derive(Clone)]
pub enum Keyword {
    Loop,
    Continue,
    Break,
    Fn,
    Extern,
}
static KEYWORDS: phf::Map<&'static str, Keyword> = phf_map! {
    "loop" => Keyword::Loop,
    "continue" => Keyword::Continue,
    "break" => Keyword::Break,
    "fn" => Keyword::Fn,
    "extern" => Keyword::Extern,
};
pub fn parse_keyword(keyword: &str) -> Option<Keyword> {
    KEYWORDS.get(keyword).cloned()
}
```
Alternatively, you can use the [ phf_codegen](https://docs.rs/phf_codegen) crate to generate PHF datatypes
in a build script.

[§](https://docs.rs#note)Note

Currently, the macro syntax has some limitations and may not
work as you want. See [#196](https://github.com/rust-phf/rust-phf/issues/196) for example.

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [map](https://docs.rs/map/index.html)
- An immutable map constructed at compile time.
- [ordered_](https://docs.rs/ordered_map/index.html)- map
- An order-preserving immutable map constructed at compile time.
- [ordered_](https://docs.rs/ordered_set/index.html)- set
- An order-preserving immutable set constructed at compile time.
- [set](https://docs.rs/set/index.html)
- An immutable set constructed at compile time.

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [phf_map](https://docs.rs/macro.phf_map.html)
- Macro to create a `static`(compile-time)`Map`
- [phf_](https://docs.rs/macro.phf_ordered_map.html)- ordered_ - map
- Macro to create a `static`(compile-time)`OrderedMap`
- [phf_](https://docs.rs/macro.phf_ordered_set.html)- ordered_ - set
- Macro to create a `static`(compile-time)`OrderedSet`
- [phf_set](https://docs.rs/macro.phf_set.html)
- Macro to create a `static`(compile-time)`Set`

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Map](https://docs.rs/struct.Map.html)
- An immutable map constructed at compile time.
- [Ordered](https://docs.rs/struct.OrderedMap.html)- Map
- An order-preserving immutable map constructed at compile time.
- [Ordered](https://docs.rs/struct.OrderedSet.html)- Set
- An order-preserving immutable set constructed at compile time.
- [Set](https://docs.rs/struct.Set.html)
- An immutable set constructed at compile time.

# phf - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/phf/0.11.3/target-redirect/i686-pc-windows-msvc/phf/

## Expand description

Rust-PHF is a library to generate efficient lookup tables at compile time using
[perfect hash functions](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perfect_hash_function).

It currently uses the
[CHD algorithm](http://cmph.sourceforge.net/papers/esa09.pdf) and can generate
a 100,000 entry map in roughly .4 seconds.

MSRV (minimum supported rust version) is Rust 1.61.

[§](https://docs.rs#usage)Usage

PHF data structures can be constructed via either the procedural
macros in the `phf_macros` crate or code generation supported by the
`phf_codegen` crate. If you prefer macros, you can easily use them by
enabling the `macros` feature of the `phf` crate, like:

```
 [dependencies]

```
To compile the `phf` crate with a dependency on
libcore instead of libstd, enabling use in environments where libstd
will not work, set `default-features = false` for the dependency:

```
[dependencies]
# to use `phf` in `no_std` environments
phf = { version = "0.11", default-features = false }
```
[§](https://docs.rs#example-with-the-macros-feature-enabled)Example (with the `macros` feature enabled)

```
use phf::phf_map;
#[derive(Clone)]

    Loop,
    Continue,
    Break,
    Fn,
    Extern,
}

    "loop" => Keyword::Loop,
    "continue" => Keyword::Continue,
    "break" => Keyword::Break,
    "fn" => Keyword::Fn,
    "extern" => Keyword::Extern,
};
pub fn parse_keyword(keyword: &str) -> Option<Keyword> {
    KEYWORDS.get(keyword).cloned()
}
```
Alternatively, you can use the [ phf_codegen](https://docs.rs/phf_codegen) crate to generate PHF datatypes
in a build script.

[§](https://docs.rs#note)Note

Currently, the macro syntax has some limitations and may not
work as you want. See [#183](https://github.com/rust-phf/rust-phf/issues/183) or [#196](https://github.com/rust-phf/rust-phf/issues/196) for example.

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [map](https://docs.rs/map/index.html)
- An immutable map constructed at compile time.
- [ordered_](https://docs.rs/ordered_map/index.html)- map
- An order-preserving immutable map constructed at compile time.
- [ordered_](https://docs.rs/ordered_set/index.html)- set
- An order-preserving immutable set constructed at compile time.
- [set](https://docs.rs/set/index.html)
- An immutable set constructed at compile time.

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [phf_map](https://docs.rs/macro.phf_map.html)
- Macro to create a `static`(compile-time)`Map`

- Macro to create a `static`(compile-time)`Set`

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- An immutable map constructed at compile time.
- [Ordered](https://docs.rs/struct.OrderedMap.html)- Map
- An order-preserving immutable map constructed at compile time.

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/phf/0.11.3/target-redirect/x86_64-pc-windows-msvc/phf/

Rust-PHF is a library to generate efficient lookup tables at compile time using
[perfect hash functions](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perfect_hash_function).

It currently uses the
[CHD algorithm](http://cmph.sourceforge.net/papers/esa09.pdf) and can generate
a 100,000 entry map in roughly .4 seconds.

MSRV (minimum supported rust version) is Rust 1.61.

```
use phf::phf_map;

pub enum Keyword {
    Loop,
    Continue,
    Break,
    Fn,
    Extern,
}
static KEYWORDS: phf::Map<&'static str, Keyword> = phf_map! {
    "loop" => Keyword::Loop,
    "continue" => Keyword::Continue,
    "break" => Keyword::Break,
    "fn" => Keyword::Fn,
    "extern" => Keyword::Extern,
};
pub fn parse_keyword(keyword: &str) -> Option<Keyword> {
    KEYWORDS.get(keyword).cloned()
}
```
Alternatively, you can use the [ phf_codegen](https://docs.rs/phf_codegen) crate to generate PHF datatypes
in a build script.

[§](https://docs.rs#note)Note

Currently, the macro syntax has some limitations and may not
work as you want. See [#183](https://github.com/rust-phf/rust-phf/issues/183) or [#196](https://github.com/rust-phf/rust-phf/issues/196) for example.

# phf - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/phf/0.11.3/target-redirect/phf/

## Expand description

Rust-PHF is a library to generate efficient lookup tables at compile time using
[perfect hash functions](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perfect_hash_function).

It currently uses the
[CHD algorithm](http://cmph.sourceforge.net/papers/esa09.pdf) and can generate
a 100,000 entry map in roughly .4 seconds.

MSRV (minimum supported rust version) is Rust 1.61.

[§](https://docs.rs#usage)Usage

PHF data structures can be constructed via either the procedural
macros in the `phf_macros` crate or code generation supported by the
`phf_codegen` crate. If you prefer macros, you can easily use them by
enabling the `macros` feature of the `phf` crate, like:

```
 [dependencies]
 phf = { version = "0.11", features = ["macros"] }
```
To compile the `phf` crate with a dependency on
libcore instead of libstd, enabling use in environments where libstd
will not work, set `default-features = false` for the dependency:

```
[dependencies]
# to use `phf` in `no_std` environments
phf = { version = "0.11", default-features = false }
```
[§](https://docs.rs#example-with-the-macros-feature-enabled)Example (with the `macros` feature enabled)

```
use phf::phf_map;
#[derive(Clone)]
pub enum Keyword {
    Loop,
    Continue,
    Break,
    Fn,
    Extern,
}
static KEYWORDS: phf::Map<&'static str, Keyword> = phf_map! {
    "loop" => Keyword::Loop,
    "continue" => Keyword::Continue,
    "break" => Keyword::Break,
    "fn" => Keyword::Fn,
    "extern" => Keyword::Extern,
};
pub fn parse_keyword(keyword: &str) -> Option<Keyword> {
    KEYWORDS.get(keyword).cloned()
}
```
Alternatively, you can use the [ phf_codegen](https://docs.rs/phf_codegen) crate to generate PHF datatypes
in a build script.

[§](https://docs.rs#note)Note

Currently, the macro syntax has some limitations and may not
work as you want. See [#183](https://github.com/rust-phf/rust-phf/issues/183) or [#196](https://github.com/rust-phf/rust-phf/issues/196) for example.

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [map](https://docs.rs/map/index.html)
- An immutable map constructed at compile time.
- [ordered_](https://docs.rs/ordered_map/index.html)- map
- An order-preserving immutable map constructed at compile time.
- [ordered_](https://docs.rs/ordered_set/index.html)- set
- An order-preserving immutable set constructed at compile time.
- [set](https://docs.rs/set/index.html)
- An immutable set constructed at compile time.

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [phf_map](https://docs.rs/macro.phf_map.html)
- Macro to create a `static`(compile-time)`Map`
- [phf_](https://docs.rs/macro.phf_ordered_map.html)- ordered_ - map
- Macro to create a `static`(compile-time)`OrderedMap`
- [phf_](https://docs.rs/macro.phf_ordered_set.html)- ordered_ - set
- Macro to create a `static`(compile-time)`OrderedSet`
- [phf_set](https://docs.rs/macro.phf_set.html)
- Macro to create a `static`(compile-time)`Set`

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Map](https://docs.rs/struct.Map.html)

- [Ordered](https://docs.rs/struct.OrderedMap.html)- Map

# phf_codegen - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/phf_codegen

## Expand description

A set of builders to generate Rust source for PHF data structures at compile time.

The provided builders are intended to be used in a Cargo build script to generate a Rust source file that will be included in a library at build time.

For more information about `rust-phf` crates, see [the  phf crate’s documentation](https://docs.rs/phf).

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

To use `phf_codegen` on build.rs, you have to add dependencies under `[build-dependencies]`:

```
[build-dependencies]
phf = { version = "0.14.0", default-features = false }
phf_codegen = "0.14.0"
```
When using the experimental `ptrhash` feature, enable it on both
`phf_codegen` and the runtime `phf` dependency so the generated constants
and runtime layout stay in sync.

Then put code on build.rs:

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
use std::env;
use std::fs::File;
use std::io::{BufWriter, Write};
use std::path::Path;
fn main() {
    let path = Path::new(&env::var("OUT_DIR").unwrap()).join("codegen.rs");
    let mut file = BufWriter::new(File::create(&path).unwrap());
    write!(
        &mut file,
        "static KEYWORDS: phf::Map<&'static str, Keyword> = {}",
        phf_codegen::Map::new()
            .entry("loop", "Keyword::Loop")
            .entry("continue", "Keyword::Continue")
            .entry("break", "Keyword::Break")
            .entry("fn", "Keyword::Fn")
            .entry("extern", "Keyword::Extern")
            .build()
    )
    .unwrap();
    write!(&mut file, ";\n").unwrap();
}
```
and lib.rs:

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
#[derive(Clone)]
enum Keyword {
    Loop,
    Continue,
    Break,
    Fn,
    Extern,
}
include!(concat!(env!("OUT_DIR"), "/codegen.rs"));
pub fn parse_keyword(keyword: &str) -> Option<Keyword> {
    KEYWORDS.get(keyword).cloned()
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#byte-string-keys)Byte-String Keys

Byte strings by default produce references to fixed-size arrays; the compiler needs a hint to coerce them to slices:

build.rs:

```
use std::env;
use std::fs::File;
use std::io::{BufWriter, Write};
use std::path::Path;
let path = Path::new(&env::var("OUT_DIR").unwrap()).join("codegen.rs");
let mut file = BufWriter::new(File::create(&path).unwrap());
writeln!(
    &mut file,
     "static KEYWORDS: phf::Map<&'static [u8], Keyword> = \n{};\n",
     phf_codegen::Map::<&[u8]>::new()
         .entry(b"loop", "Keyword::Loop")
         .entry(b"continue", "Keyword::Continue")
         .entry(b"break", "Keyword::Break")
         .entry(b"fn", "Keyword::Fn")
         .entry(b"extern", "Keyword::Extern")
         .build()
).unwrap();
```
lib.rs:

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
#[derive(Clone)]
enum Keyword {
    Loop,
    Continue,
    Break,
    Fn,
    Extern,
}
include!(concat!(env!("OUT_DIR"), "/codegen.rs"));
pub fn parse_keyword(keyword: &[u8]) -> Option<Keyword> {
    KEYWORDS.get(keyword).cloned()
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#note)Note

The compiler’s stack will overflow when processing extremely long method chains (500+ calls). When generating large PHF data structures, consider looping over the entries or making each call a separate statement:

```
let entries = [("hello", "1"), ("world", "2")];
let mut builder = phf_codegen::Map::new();
for &(key, value) in &entries {
    builder.entry(key, value);
}
// ...
```
```
let mut builder = phf_codegen::Map::new();
builder.entry("hello", "1");
builder.entry("world", "2");
// ...
```
## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Display](https://docs.rs/struct.DisplayMap.html)- Map
- An adapter for printing a `Map`
- [Display](https://docs.rs/struct.DisplayOrderedMap.html)- Ordered - Map
- An adapter for printing a `OrderedMap`

- [Ordered](https://docs.rs/struct.OrderedMap.html)- Map

- [Ordered](https://docs.rs/struct.OrderedSet.html)- Set

# phf_map in phf - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/phf/^0.11/macro.phf_map.html

`phf_map!() { /* proc-macro */ }`## Expand description

Macro to create a `static` (compile-time) [ Map](https://docs.rs/struct.Map.html).

Requires the `macros` feature.

Supported key expressions are:

- literals: bools, (byte) strings, bytes, chars, and integers (these must have a type suffix)
- arrays of `u8`integers
- dereferenced byte string literals
- `UniCase::unicode(string)`or- `UniCase::ascii(string)`if the- `unicase`feature is enabled

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use phf::{phf_map, Map};
static MY_MAP: Map<&'static str, u32> = phf_map! {
    "hello" => 1,
    "world" => 2,
};
fn main () {
    assert_eq!(MY_MAP["hello"], 1);
}
```

---

# OrderedMap in phf - Rust

`pub struct OrderedMap<K: 'static, V: 'static> { /* private fields */ }`## Expand description

An order-preserving immutable map constructed at compile time.

Unlike a `Map`, iteration order is guaranteed to match the definition
order.

[§](https://docs.rs#note)Note

The fields of this struct are public so that they may be initialized by the
`phf_ordered_map!` macro and code generation. They are subject to change at
any time and should never be accessed directly.

# PhfHash in phf - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/phf/^0.11/trait.PhfHash.html

```
pub trait PhfHash {
    // Required method
    fn
```
[phf_hash](https://docs.rs#tymethod.phf_hash)<H>(&self, state: [&mut H](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.reference.html))
       where H: [Hasher](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/hash/trait.Hasher.html);
    // Provided method
    fn [phf_hash_slice](https://docs.rs#method.phf_hash_slice)<H>(data: &[Self], state: [&mut H](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.reference.html))
       where H: [Hasher](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/hash/trait.Hasher.html),
             Self: [Sized](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/marker/trait.Sized.html) { ... }
}## Expand description

A trait implemented by types which can be used in PHF data structures.

This differs from the standard library’s `Hash` trait in that `PhfHash`’s
results must be architecture independent so that hashes will be consistent
between the host and target when cross compiling.

## Required Methods[§](https://docs.rs#required-methods)

## Provided Methods[§](https://docs.rs#provided-methods)

## Dyn Compatibility[§](https://docs.rs#dyn-compatibility)

This trait is **not** [dyn compatible](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/reference/items/traits.html#dyn-compatibility).

*In older versions of Rust, dyn compatibility was called "object safety", so this trait is not object safe.*

# unicase 2.9.0 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/unicase/2.9.0

# unicase

Compare strings when case is not important (using Unicode Case-folding).

```
// ignore ASCII case
let a = new;
let b = new;
assert_eq!;
// using unicode case-folding
let c = new
let d = new;
assert_eq!;
```

                    unicase 2.9.0

# unicase - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/unicase/2.9.0/target-redirect/unicase/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#unicase)UniCase

UniCase provides a way of specifying strings that are case-insensitive.

UniCase supports full [Unicode case
folding](https://www.w3.org/International/wiki/Case_folding). It can also
utilize faster ASCII case comparisons, if both strings are ASCII.

Using the `UniCase::new()` constructor will check the string to see if it
is all ASCII. When a `UniCase` is compared against another, if both are
ASCII, it will use the faster comparison.

There also exists the `Ascii` type in this crate, which will always assume
to use the ASCII case comparisons, if the encoding is already known.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use unicase::UniCase;
let a = UniCase::new("Maße");
let b = UniCase::new("MASSE");
let c = UniCase::new("mase");
assert_eq!(a, b);
assert!(b != c);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#ascii)Ascii

```
use unicase::Ascii;
let a = Ascii::new("foobar");
let b = Ascii::new("FoObAr");
assert_eq!(a, b);
```

# eq in unicase - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/unicase/^2.8.1/fn.eq.html

## Expand description

Compare two string-like types for case-less equality, using unicode folding.

Equivalent to `UniCase::new(left) == UniCase::new(right)`.

Note: This will perform a scan for ASCII characters before doing the
the comparison. See `UniCase` for more information.

---

# eq_ascii in unicase - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/unicase/^2.8.1/fn.eq_ascii.html

## Expand description

Compare two string-like types for case-less equality, ignoring ASCII case.

Equivalent to `Ascii::new(left) == Ascii::new(right)`.

# cfg_if - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/cfg-if/^1/

## Expand description

A macro for defining `#[cfg]` if-else statements.

The macro provided by this crate, `cfg_if`, is similar to the `if/elif` C
preprocessor macro by allowing definition of a cascade of `#[cfg]` cases,
emitting the implementation which matches first.

This allows you to conveniently provide a long list `#[cfg]`’d blocks of code
without having to rewrite each clause multiple times.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
cfg_if::cfg_if! {
    if #[cfg(unix)] {
        fn foo() { /* unix specific functionality */ }
    } else if #[cfg(target_pointer_width = "32")] {
        fn foo() { /* non-unix, 32-bit functionality */ }
    } else {
        fn foo() { /* fallback implementation */ }
    }
}
```
## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [cfg_if](https://docs.rs/macro.cfg_if.html)
- The main macro provided by this crate. See crate documentation for more information.

# clap - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/clap/^4/

## Expand description

Command Line Argument Parser for Rust

Quick Links:

- Derive [tutorial](https://docs.rs/_derive/_tutorial/index.html)and[reference](https://docs.rs/_derive/index.html)
- Builder [tutorial](https://docs.rs/_tutorial/index.html)and[reference](https://docs.rs/struct.Command.html)
- [Cookbook](https://docs.rs/_cookbook/index.html)
- [CLI Concepts](https://docs.rs/_concepts/index.html)
- [FAQ](https://docs.rs/_faq/index.html)
- [Discussions](https://github.com/clap-rs/clap/discussions)
- [CHANGELOG](https://github.com/clap-rs/clap/blob/v4.6.1/CHANGELOG.md)(includes major version migration guides)

[§](https://docs.rs#aspirations)Aspirations

- Out of the box, users get a polished CLI experience
- Including common argument behavior, help generation, suggested fixes for users, colored output, [shell completions](https://github.com/clap-rs/clap/tree/master/clap_complete), etc

- Including common argument behavior, help generation, suggested fixes for users, colored output,
- Flexible enough to port your existing CLI interface
- However, we won’t necessarily streamline support for each use case

- Reasonable parse performance
- Resilient maintainership, including
- Willing to break compatibility rather than batching up breaking changes in large releases
- Leverage feature flags to keep to one active branch
- Being under [WG-CLI](https://github.com/rust-cli/team/)to increase the bus factor

- We follow semver and will wait about 6-9 months between major breaking changes
- We will support the last two minor Rust releases (MSRV, currently 1.74)

While these aspirations can be at odds with fast build times and low binary
size, we will still strive to keep these reasonable for the flexibility you
get.  Check out the
[argparse-benchmarks](https://github.com/rust-cli/argparse-benchmarks-rs) for
CLI parsers optimized for other use cases.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

Run

`$ cargo add clap --features derive`*(See also  feature flag reference)*

Then define your CLI in `main.rs`:

```
use clap::Parser;
/// Simple program to greet a person
#[derive(Parser, Debug)]
#[command(version, about, long_about = None)]
struct Args {
    /// Name of the person to greet
    #[arg(short, long)]
    name: String,
    /// Number of times to greet
    #[arg(short, long, default_value_t = 1)]
    count: u8,
}
fn main() {
    let args = Args::parse();
    for _ in 0..args.count {
        println!("Hello {}!", args.name);
    }
}
```
And try it out:

```
$ demo --help
A simple to use, efficient, and full-featured Command Line Argument Parser
Usage: demo[EXE] [OPTIONS] --name <NAME>
Options:
  -n, --name <NAME>    Name of the person to greet
  -c, --count <COUNT>  Number of times to greet [default: 1]
  -h, --help           Print help
  -V, --version        Print version
$ demo --name Me
Hello Me!
```
*(version number and  .exe extension on windows replaced by placeholders)*

See also the derive [tutorial](https://docs.rs/_derive/_tutorial/index.html) and [reference](https://docs.rs/_derive/index.html)

[§](https://docs.rs#related-projects)Related Projects

Augment clap:

- [wild](https://crates.io/crates/wild)for supporting wildcards (- `*`) on Windows like you do Linux
- [argfile](https://crates.io/crates/argfile)for loading additional arguments from a file (aka response files)
- [shadow-rs](https://crates.io/crates/shadow-rs)for generating- `Command::long_version`
- [clap_mangen](https://crates.io/crates/clap_mangen)for generating man page source (roff)
- [clap_complete](https://crates.io/crates/clap_complete)for shell completion support
- [clap-i18n-richformatter](https://crates.io/crates/clap-i18n-richformatter)for i18n support with- `clap::error::RichFormatter`

CLI Helpers

- [clio](https://crates.io/crates/clio)for reading/writing to files specified as arguments
- [clap-verbosity-flag](https://crates.io/crates/clap-verbosity-flag)

Testing

- `trycmd`

Documentation:

# condtype - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/condtype/^1.3/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#condtype)`condtype`

Choose Rust types at compile-time via boolean constants, brought to you by
[Nikolai Vazquez](https://hachyderm.io/@nikolai).

If you find this library useful, consider
[starring it](https://github.com/nvzqz/condtype) as well as
[sponsoring](https://github.com/sponsors/nvzqz) or
[donating once](https://paypal.me/nvzqz). 💖

[§](https://docs.rs#conditional-typing)Conditional Typing

The [ CondType](https://docs.rs/type.CondType.html) type and

[macro choose types at compile-time using](https://docs.rs/macro.condval.html)

`condval!`[constants, just like](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.bool.html)

`bool`[. Unlike the](https://en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/types/conditional)

`std::conditional_t` in C++[type, the type chosen by](https://docs.rs/either/latest/either/enum.Either.html)

`Either`[/](https://docs.rs/type.CondType.html)

`CondType`[is directly used, rather than wrapped with an](https://docs.rs/macro.condval.html)

`condval!`[type. This may be considered a form of](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/keyword.enum.html)

`enum`[dependent typing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dependent_type), but it is limited in ability and is restricted to compile-time constants rather than runtime values.

[§](https://docs.rs#condtype-1)`CondType`

In the following example, [ CondType](https://docs.rs/type.CondType.html) aliases either

[or](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.str.html)

`&str`[, depending on the boolean](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.i32.html)

`i32`[generic constant](https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/items/generics.html#const-generics):

```
use condtype::CondType;
let str: CondType<true,  &str, i32> = "hello";
let int: CondType<false, &str, i32> = 42;
// Unsized types are also supported:
let str: &CondType<true, str, [u8]> = "world";
```
[§](https://docs.rs#condval)`condval!`

[ condval!](https://docs.rs/macro.condval.html) enables choosing differently-typed values without specifying types.
In the following example,

`val` is inferred to be either [or](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.str.html)

`&str`[, depending on](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.i32.html)

`i32``COND`.```
use condtype::condval;
const COND: bool = true;
let val = condval!(if COND {
    "hello"
} else {
    42
});
assert_eq!(val, "hello");
```
`if let` pattern matching is also supported:

```
use condtype::condval;
const STR: Option<&str> = Some("hello");
let val = condval!(if let Some(str) = STR {
    str.to_uppercase()
} else {
    42
});
assert_eq!(val, "HELLO");
```
[§](https://docs.rs#platform-specific-types)Platform-Specific Types

This library can make code for some platforms more efficient by using smaller-sized types, depending on platform-specific constants.

In the following example, the `RlimOption` type can be either
[Option](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html)<[rlim_t](https://pubs.opengroup.org/onlinepubs/9699919799/basedefs/sys_resource.h.html)>[ rlim_t](https://pubs.opengroup.org/onlinepubs/9699919799/basedefs/sys_resource.h.html) itself,
where

[can be treated as a sentinel value for](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u64.html#associatedconstant.MAX)

`rlim_t::MAX`[if it is not equal to](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html#variant.None)

`Option::None`[.](https://pubs.opengroup.org/onlinepubs/9699919799/basedefs/sys_resource.h.html)

`RLIM_INFINITY````
use condtype::{condval, CondType};
use libc::{rlim_t, RLIM_INFINITY};
const RLIM_INFINITY_IS_MAX: bool = RLIM_INFINITY == rlim_t::MAX;
type RlimOption = CondType<RLIM_INFINITY_IS_MAX, Option<rlim_t>, rlim_t>;
const RLIM_NONE: RlimOption = condval!(if RLIM_INFINITY_IS_MAX {
    None::<rlim_t>
} else {
    rlim_t::MAX
});
// Convert from either `RlimOption` type to `Option` via the `Into` trait:
let rlim_none: Option<rlim_t> = RLIM_NONE.into();
```
Without this library, one could otherwise use [ cfg_if!](https://docs.rs/cfg-if/latest/cfg_if/macro.cfg_if.html) to achieve the same
goal. However, using

[requires maintaining a list of platforms and being more fine-grained if](https://doc.rust-lang.org/rust-by-example/attribute/cfg.html)

`#[cfg]`[is dependent on CPU architecture.](https://pubs.opengroup.org/onlinepubs/9699919799/basedefs/sys_resource.h.html)

`RLIM_INFINITY````
use cfg_if::cfg_if;
use libc::rlim_t;
cfg_if! {
    // Platforms where `RLIM_INFINITY != rlim_t::MAX`:
    if #[cfg(any(
        target_os = "macos",
        target_os = "freebsd",
        target_os = "solaris",
        // ad nauseam...
    ))] {
        type RlimOption = rlim_t;
        const RLIM_NONE: RlimOption = rlim_t::MAX;
    } else {
        type RlimOption = Option<rlim_t>;
        const RLIM_NONE: RlimOption = None;
    }
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#limitations)Limitations

It is currently not possible to use [ CondType](https://docs.rs/type.CondType.html) or

[with a](https://docs.rs/macro.condval.html)

`condval!`[generic constant](https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/items/generics.html#const-generics)because

[Rust does not yet consider trait implementations based on booleans to be exhaustive](https://github.com/rust-lang/project-const-generics/issues/26). Once that issue is resolved, all versions of this library should

*just work*with generic constants.

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
fn generic<const B: bool>() {
    let val: CondType<B, &str, i32> = condval!(if B {
        "hello"
    } else {
        42
    });
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#install)Install

This library is [available on crates.io](https://crates.io/crates/condtype) and
can be used by running the following `cargo` command in your project directory:

`cargo add condtype`or by manually adding the following to your project’s [ Cargo.toml](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/manifest.html):

```
[dependencies]
condtype = "1.3.0"
```

- Instantiates a [conditionally-typed](https://docs.rs/index.html#conditional-typing)value.
